subtopics.title: Operating System Basics: Tasks, Processes & Threads
subtopics.subtitle: OS and kernel roles, RTOS vs GPOS, process states, threads and context switching

concepts.text: What an Operating System Does

An operating system (OS) is the software layer that manages hardware resources (CPU time, memory, I/O devices, files) and provides services to application programs. It hides hardware details behind system calls, shares the CPU among many activities, protects programs from each other and handles interrupts. In an embedded system the OS is often a small real-time kernel linked with the application into one firmware image.
Kernel space vs user space:
items: Kernel space: privileged (supervisor) mode; the kernel can execute every instruction and access all memory and device registers.
User space: unprivileged mode; applications reach hardware only through system calls, which trap into the kernel.
Monolithic kernels (e.g. Linux) put drivers and services in kernel space; microkernels (e.g. QNX) keep only scheduling, IPC and basic memory management in the kernel.
Many small RTOSes (FreeRTOS, uC/OS on MCUs without an MMU) run tasks and kernel in one address space, trading protection for speed and simplicity.

concepts.text: RTOS vs General-Purpose OS

rows: Bounded, small interrupt and dispatch latency
Variable, may be long under load

concepts.text: Classes of real-time systems (by the cost of a missed deadline):
items: Hard real-time: missing a deadline is a system failure (airbag deployment, pacemaker, flight control).
Firm real-time: a late result is useless and discarded, but occasional misses are tolerated (video frame decoding).
Soft real-time: late results still have reduced value; quality degrades gracefully (audio streaming, online games).
Real-time means correct AND on time: determinism matters more than raw speed.

concepts.text: Tasks, Processes and the PCB

A program is passive code on disk or flash; a process is a program in execution with its own address space, stack, registers and resources. In an RTOS the schedulable unit is usually called a task, which behaves like a thread. The kernel keeps a Process (or Task) Control Block (PCB/TCB) for each one, holding the process ID, state, priority, saved program counter and registers, stack pointer, memory limits, open files/resources and accounting information.

rows: Can run, waiting for the CPU
Pre-empted to Ready; waits to Blocked; exits to Terminated
Waiting for an event, I/O, delay or semaphore
Shared with other threads of the process
A crash can bring down the whole process

concepts.text: Context Switch and Interrupt Timing

A context switch saves the state (registers, PC, stack pointer, status word) of the running task in its TCB and restores the state of the next task chosen by the scheduler. It is pure overhead: no useful work is done during the switch, so an RTOS keeps it short and bounded. Interrupt latency is the time from an interrupt request to the first instruction of its ISR; it grows when interrupts are disabled for long periods inside the kernel or drivers.

concepts.plainText: Interrupt response time = interrupt latency + ISR execution time

concepts.text: Kernel objects an RTOS typically provides:
items: Tasks/threads with fixed priorities and their TCBs and stacks.
Semaphores (binary and counting) and mutexes for synchronisation.
Message queues, mailboxes, pipes and event flags for communication.
Software timers, delays and tick counter (system tick, e.g. 1 ms).
Memory pools with fixed-size blocks for deterministic allocation.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Kernels, Task States and Switching Cost

An embedded OS differs from a desktop OS less in its ideas than in its priorities. It is configured when the firmware is built, so only the kernel objects the application uses are linked in, and the image runs from Flash with a few kilobytes of RAM. Tasks, stacks and queues are often created statically at start-up; there is usually no disk, no demand paging and no MMU, and every kernel service is written so that its worst-case execution time is known. A GPOS instead optimises average throughput and fairness, and paging, dynamic memory allocation and long non-pre-emptible kernel paths make its worst case large and hard to bound.

rows: Scheduler, memory manager, drivers, file systems, network stack
Only scheduling, IPC, basic memory management and interrupt dispatch
One system call; services call each other directly
Message to a user-space server and a reply, with extra mode and context switches
Slower per request because of IPC
Confined to its server process, which can be restarted

concepts.text: Determinism means that every kernel service and every path from an event to its response has a known upper bound; it does not mean that the average is fast. Between an external event and the first instruction of the task that handles it, four delays add up: interrupt latency (hardware recognition plus any time interrupts are disabled), ISR execution, the scheduler's decision and the context switch, the last two together being the scheduling or dispatch latency. The variation of these delays from one occurrence to the next is called jitter. RTOS kernels keep the scheduler O(1), for example with one bit per priority level in a ready bitmap whose highest set bit is found by a count-leading-zeros instruction, so dispatch time does not grow with the number of tasks.

concepts.plainText: Event-to-task latency = interrupt latency + ISR execution time + scheduler time + context-switch time

rows: Scheduler dispatches the highest-priority ready task
Kernel decision after a tick, ISR or API call
Pre-empted by a higher-priority task, or its time slice ends
taskYIELD() or a tick with equal-priority tasks ready
Waits for a delay, semaphore, queue or event
The awaited event occurs or the timeout expires

concepts.text: What the kernel keeps for each task, and where:
items: TCB: task ID or name, state, current and base priority, saved stack pointer (or saved registers), stack base and size, links into the ready or waiting lists, the event or timeout being waited for, and statistics such as run time.

Context: program counter, stack pointer, status register and general-purpose registers, plus FPU registers if the task uses floating point; many small kernels push it onto the task's own stack and keep only the stack pointer in the TCB.
Not in the TCB: the task's code, which stays in Flash or the process image, and its local variables, which live on its stack.
A GPOS process control block adds the memory map (page-table pointer), open-file table, signal handlers and parent/child links; a thread control block holds only the per-thread part.

concepts.text:
Context-switch time on an 80 MHz CPU (12.5 ns per cycle)
save 16 registers + restore 16 registers = 32 transfers
32 transfers x 1 cycle              = 32 cycles
exception entry/exit + scheduler    = 48 cycles
t_cs = (32 + 48) x 12.5 ns          = 1.0 µs
RAM for 6 tasks: TCB 80 B, stack 512 B (1 KB = 1024 B)
6 x (80 + 512) = 3552 B = 3.47 KB
each stack must also leave room for one saved frame: 16 x 4 B = 64 B

Round robin: q = 10 ms, t_cs = 0.2 ms
overhead = t_cs / (q + t_cs) = 0.2 / 10.2 = 1.96 %
smallest q for overhead <= 5 %: q >= t_cs (1 - 0.05) / 0.05 = 3.8 ms
RTOS load: 1 kHz tick at 4 µs, 300 switches/s at 5 µs
per second: 1000 x 4 µs + 300 x 5 µs = 4.0 ms + 1.5 ms = 5.5 ms
overhead = 5.5 ms / 1000 ms = 0.55 %
32-bit tick counter at 1 kHz wraps after 2^32 ms = 49.7 days

Threads can be provided by a user-space library or by the kernel itself. In the many-to-one model the kernel sees one thread per process, so switching is cheap, but a blocking system call stops every thread and two threads can never run on two cores at once; the one-to-one model of Linux and Windows maps each thread to a kernel thread and removes both limits at the cost of a kernel call per thread operation, and the many-to-many model multiplexes user threads over a pool of kernel threads. In an RTOS every task is effectively a kernel-level thread, and all tasks share one address space. Multithreading brings responsiveness (one thread waits for I/O while another runs), cheap data sharing, lower creation and switching cost than processes, and parallel speed-up on multicore chips.
Common mistakes and special cases:
items: Blocked never goes straight to Running, and Ready never goes to Blocked: a task must be running to ask to wait.
Round-robin overhead is t_cs / (q + t_cs), not t_cs / q; the two differ noticeably when the slice is short.
With n tasks in round robin, a task waits (n − 1) slices plus n switches before it runs again, because the switch back to it counts too.
A delay of n ticks blocks for between n − 1 and n tick periods, because the call happens part-way through a tick.
A thread switch inside one process is cheaper than a process switch because the address space, page tables and TLB stay the same, but the registers must still be saved.
Firm real-time: a late result is worthless but occasional misses are tolerated; soft real-time: a late result still has some value.

concepts.text: For overhead questions, draw the time line slice, switch, slice, switch, and count every switch, including the one back to the task you are following. Convert cycles to time with t = cycles / f_clk, and add per-second costs (rate × duration) before dividing by one second.

formulas.plainText: Response time = interrupt latency + ISR execution time
Context-switch overhead = t_cs / (q + t_cs), q = time slice
Waiting time = turnaround time - CPU burst time

notes.text: Remember the three items a thread owns privately: program counter, register set and stack. Everything else (code, data, heap, open files) is shared with sibling threads.
Real-time does not mean fast. An RTOS is judged by worst-case, bounded response time; a GPOS may be faster on average yet still unsuitable for hard deadlines.
Running to Ready happens on pre-emption or time-slice expiry; Running to Blocked happens when the task waits for I/O, a delay or a semaphore; Blocked never goes directly to Running.

formulas.title: Interrupt response time
formulas.plainText: Response time = interrupt latency + ISR execution time
formulas.description: Total time from an interrupt request until its service routine has finished.

formulas.title: Context-switch overhead
formulas.plainText: Overhead = t_cs / (q + t_cs)
formulas.description: Fraction of CPU time lost to switching when each time slice q is followed by a switch of length t_cs.

formulas.title: Waiting time
formulas.plainText: Waiting time = turnaround time - burst time
formulas.description: Time a task spends in the ready queue, where turnaround = completion time - arrival time.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between hard and soft real-time systems?
flashcards.back: In hard real-time a missed deadline is a system failure (e.g. airbag); in soft real-time a late result still has some value and only quality degrades (e.g. audio streaming).

flashcards.front: What does a Process/Task Control Block (PCB/TCB) store?
flashcards.back: Process ID, state, priority, saved PC and registers, stack pointer, memory limits, resource/open-file list and accounting information.

flashcards.front: What is private to each thread of a process?
flashcards.back: Its program counter, register set and stack; code, data, heap and open files are shared.
The time from an interrupt request until the first instruction of its ISR executes; long interrupt-disabled sections increase it.

questions.questionText: An automotive airbag controller must fire within 15 ms of a crash; firing later is considered a system failure. This is an example of:
options: Soft real-time system
Hard real-time system
Batch processing system
Time-sharing system
questions.explanation: When missing a deadline counts as failure, the system is hard real-time. Soft real-time systems tolerate late results with degraded quality.

questions.questionText: A running task has its time slice expire and is pre-empted by the scheduler. Which state does it move to?
options: Blocked
Terminated
Ready
New
questions.explanation: A pre-empted task is still able to run, so it returns to the Ready queue. Blocked is only for tasks waiting on an event or I/O.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT shared among threads of the same process?
options: Global data
Code section
Open files
Stack
questions.explanation: Each thread has its own stack, program counter and registers; code, global data, heap and open files are shared by all threads of the process.

questions.questionText: An RTOS has an interrupt latency of 12 µs and the ISR takes 30 µs to execute. What is the interrupt response time (to ISR completion)?
options: 18 µs
30 µs
42 µs
360 µs
questions.explanation: Response time = latency + ISR execution time = 12 + 30 = 42 µs.

questions.questionText: Which feature is typical of an embedded RTOS kernel but not of a desktop general-purpose OS?
options: It relies on demand paging of programs from a disk
It schedules mainly for fairness and high average throughput
It needs gigabytes of RAM and a large file system to boot
It is configured at build time so that only the needed kernel services are linked into a small Flash image
questions.explanation: An embedded RTOS is scaled to the application when the firmware is built and runs from ROM or Flash with little RAM. Demand paging, fairness-oriented scheduling and large memory needs describe a desktop GPOS.

questions.questionText: An RTOS kernel is described as deterministic. What does this mean?
options: Its average response time is the lowest of any operating system
It runs tasks strictly in the order in which they were created
Its services and responses take a known, bounded worst-case time
It keeps interrupts disabled so that tasks are never disturbed
questions.explanation: Determinism is about predictability: the worst-case time of every kernel service and response path is bounded and known. It says nothing about the average being low.

questions.questionText: A 1 ms periodic control task is released by a timer. Measurements show that it starts between 12 µs and 47 µs after each nominal release instant. What is its start (release) jitter?
options: 47 µs
59 µs
35 µs
questions.explanation: Jitter is the variation of the delay: 47 − 12 = 35 µs. 47 µs is the worst-case latency, 59 µs adds the two values and 29.5 µs is their average.

questions.questionText: A hard real-time interrupt must be serviced within 50 µs. RTOS A has an average interrupt latency of 2 µs and a worst case of 200 µs; RTOS B has an average of 6 µs and a worst case of 15 µs. Which should be chosen?
options: A, because its average latency is three times lower
Either, because both average latencies are well below 50 µs
B, because only its worst-case latency is guaranteed to meet the deadline
Neither, because the deadline must exceed the sum of both worst cases
questions.explanation: A hard deadline must be met every time, so the worst case decides: 15 µs < 50 µs for B, while A can take up to 200 µs. Average figures are irrelevant for hard real time.

questions.questionText: In a monolithic kernel such as Linux, where do device drivers, file systems and the network stack run?
options: In separate user-space server processes that exchange messages
In firmware inside each device controller
In kernel space, in the same address space as the scheduler
In the bootloader, before the kernel starts
questions.explanation: A monolithic kernel places all OS services in privileged kernel space, where they call each other directly. User-space servers are the microkernel approach.

questions.questionText: What is the main reliability advantage of a microkernel (for example QNX Neutrino) over a monolithic kernel?
options: Every service request is a direct function call, so there is no IPC overhead
All code runs in supervisor mode, so protection faults cannot occur
It needs no scheduler, because each server polls for work
Drivers and services run as separate user-space processes, so a faulty driver can be restarted without crashing the kernel
questions.explanation: A microkernel keeps only scheduling, IPC and basic memory management in the kernel, so a crashing driver is isolated in its own address space. The price is extra IPC and context switches per request.

questions.questionText: A driver request in a monolithic kernel costs one system call. In a microkernel the same request additionally needs 2 IPC messages (request and reply) of 3 µs each and 2 extra context switches of 4 µs each. At 2,500 requests per second, what extra fraction of CPU time does the microkernel spend?
questions.explanation: Extra per request = 2 × 3 + 2 × 4 = 14 µs; per second 2,500 × 14 µs = 35 ms, which is 3.5 % of one second. 2.0 % counts only the switches, 1.5 % only the messages and 1.75 % one of each.

questions.questionText: Which statement best distinguishes a process from a program?
options: A process is the source code, and a program is its compiled form
A process is a program stored in Flash rather than on disk
A program and a process are two names for the same thing
A process is a program in execution, with its own state, address space and resources tracked by the OS
questions.explanation: A program is passive code; it becomes a process when loaded and run, gaining a PCB, an address space, a stack, register state and resources.

questions.questionText: A thread is best described as:
options: A separate process with its own protected address space
A unit of execution within a process that has its own PC, registers and stack but shares the process's code, data and files
A hardware interrupt service routine
A block of memory reserved for inter-process communication
questions.explanation: Threads are the schedulable units inside a process; each has a private execution context and stack, while code, global data, heap and open files are shared.

questions.questionText: A system runs 3 processes, each with 4 threads. Ignoring kernel stacks, how many thread stacks and how many separate address spaces exist?
options: 12 stacks and 3 address spaces
3 stacks and 12 address spaces
12 stacks and 12 address spaces
3 stacks and 3 address spaces
questions.explanation: Every thread has its own stack, 3 × 4 = 12, while all threads of a process share its address space, giving 3 address spaces.

questions.questionText: In the five-state model, which state does a newly created task enter once the kernel has admitted it?
options: Running
Blocked
Ready
Terminated
questions.explanation: Admission moves a task from New to Ready, where it waits for the scheduler to dispatch it; it reaches Running only when dispatched.

questions.questionText: In the five-state task model (New, Ready, Running, Blocked, Terminated), which transition can never occur directly?
options: Ready → Blocked
Running → Blocked
Blocked → Ready
Running → Ready
questions.explanation: A task can only start waiting by executing a wait request, which requires it to be running, so Ready → Blocked is impossible. The other three are the normal wait, wake-up and pre-emption transitions.

questions.questionText: A running FreeRTOS task calls the delay function vTaskDelay(100) to wait 100 ticks. Which state does it enter?
options: Ready
Blocked
Suspended
Terminated
questions.explanation: Waiting for time, a semaphore or a queue moves the task to Blocked until the timeout or event occurs. In FreeRTOS, Suspended is entered only by an explicit vTaskSuspend() call.

questions.questionText: In a pre-emptive priority-based RTOS, low-priority task L is running when an ISR gives a semaphore on which high-priority task H is blocked. What happens when the ISR exits, assuming it requests a context switch?
options: H moves Blocked → Running directly, and L moves to Blocked
H moves Blocked → Ready → Running, and L moves Running → Ready
H moves to Ready and waits until L blocks or finishes
L continues, and H moves to Suspended until L's time slice ends
questions.explanation: The semaphore makes H ready; since H now has the highest priority among ready tasks, the scheduler pre-empts L, which goes back to Ready (not Blocked, since it is not waiting). Waiting for L would be cooperative behaviour.

questions.questionText: In FreeRTOS, how does the Suspended state differ from the Blocked state?
options: A suspended task is still considered by the scheduler at its normal priority
A suspended task has no timeout and leaves the state only when another task or an ISR explicitly resumes it
A suspended task has been deleted and its TCB freed
A suspended task is waiting for a semaphore with a timeout
questions.explanation: Blocked tasks wait for an event or a timeout; suspended tasks are ignored by the scheduler until vTaskResume() or xTaskResumeFromISR() is called.

questions.questionText: What is the idle task in an RTOS?
options: The highest-priority task, which runs first after reset
A task that has been blocked for longer than its timeout
The ISR that handles the system tick
A lowest-priority task created by the kernel that runs whenever no other task is ready
questions.explanation: The kernel always needs something to run, so it creates an idle task at the lowest priority; it often puts the CPU into a low-power mode or performs housekeeping.

questions.questionText: Which item is normally NOT stored in a task's control block (TCB)?
options: The saved stack pointer or saved register context
The task's current state and priority
The machine code of the task's function
Links to the ready or waiting list the task belongs to
questions.explanation: The TCB describes the task (state, priority, saved context, list links, stack limits); the code itself stays in Flash or the process image and is only referenced through the saved program counter.

questions.questionText: In many small RTOSes, a context switch pushes the pre-empted task's registers onto that task's own stack and stores only the stack pointer in its TCB. What does this imply for stack sizing?
options: Only the idle task needs a stack, because the other tasks share it
Stacks can be made smaller, because registers are no longer stored anywhere
The TCB must grow to hold a copy of every register of every task
Every task's stack must have room for a full saved register frame on top of the task's own worst-case usage
questions.explanation: Because the context lives on the task's stack whenever the task is not running, each stack needs its own worst-case depth plus one saved frame (and any interrupt frames that land on it).

questions.questionText: Which sequence correctly describes a context switch?
options: Restore the next task's context, then save the current task's context, then run the scheduler
Select the next task, discard the current task's registers and start the next task from its first instruction
Flush all caches, reboot the kernel and start the highest-priority task
Save the running task's context in its TCB or stack, let the scheduler select the next task, restore that task's context, and resume it at its saved PC
questions.explanation: The outgoing context must be saved before registers are overwritten, and the incoming task continues where it left off, at the PC saved in its context.

questions.questionText: Why is switching between two threads of the same process usually faster than switching between two processes?
options: Threads have no registers, so nothing needs to be saved
Thread switches are done entirely by hardware, without kernel code
Threads of one process always run on different CPU cores
The threads share one address space, so the memory map (page tables) need not change and TLB and cache contents stay useful
questions.explanation: A process switch must also switch the memory map, which invalidates TLB entries and cools the caches; a thread switch saves and restores only the register context and stack pointer.

questions.questionText: A context switch on an 80 MHz processor saves 16 registers and restores 16 registers. Each register transfer to or from memory takes 2 clock cycles, and exception entry/exit plus the scheduler add 40 cycles. What is the context-switch time?
options: 0.9 µs
1.3 µs
0.8 µs
2.1 µs
questions.explanation: Cycles = 32 transfers × 2 + 40 = 104, and 104 / 80 MHz = 1.3 µs. 0.9 µs counts only the saves, 0.8 µs leaves out the 40 cycles and 2.1 µs uses 4 cycles per transfer.

questions.questionText: Under round-robin scheduling each time slice of q = 20 ms is followed by a context switch lasting 0.5 ms. What percentage of CPU time is lost to switching?
questions.explanation: Overhead = t_cs / (q + t_cs) = 0.5 / 20.5 = 2.44 %. 2.50 % divides by q alone, and 97.56 % is the useful fraction.

questions.questionText: A context switch takes 0.5 ms. What is the smallest round-robin time slice q that keeps the switching overhead t_cs / (q + t_cs) at or below 20 %?
options: 2.5 ms
2.0 ms
0.1 ms
0.4 ms
questions.explanation: t_cs / (q + t_cs) ≤ 0.2 gives q ≥ t_cs × (1 − 0.2) / 0.2 = 0.5 × 4 = 2.0 ms. 2.5 ms comes from t_cs / q ≤ 0.2, while 0.1 ms and 0.4 ms multiply t_cs by 0.2 and 0.8.

questions.questionText: Five equal-priority tasks share the CPU round robin with a 10 ms time slice, and every context switch takes 2 ms. When a task's slice ends, how long does it wait before it runs again if every other task uses its full slice?
options: 48 ms
50 ms
40 ms
60 ms
questions.explanation: The other 4 tasks run one slice each and there are 5 switches (including the one back to the task): 4 × 10 + 5 × 2 = 50 ms. 48 ms misses the last switch, 40 ms ignores switching and 60 ms counts five slices.

questions.questionText: An RTOS has a 1 kHz tick whose handler takes 8 µs, performs 400 context switches per second at 5 µs each, and services a 2 kHz sensor interrupt whose ISR takes 15 µs. What percentage of CPU time remains for the tasks?
questions.explanation: Per second: 1000 × 8 µs + 400 × 5 µs + 2000 × 15 µs = 8 + 2 + 30 = 40 ms, so 1000 − 40 = 960 ms (96.0 %) is left. 99.0 % forgets the ISR, 97.5 % runs the ISR at 1 kHz and 4.0 % is the overhead itself.

questions.questionText: A system performs 4,000 context switches per second. A switch between processes costs 25 µs, while a switch between threads of one process costs 5 µs. If the design is changed from processes to threads, how much CPU time is saved?
options: 10 % (100 ms per second)
2 % (20 ms per second)
8 % (80 ms per second)
0.8 % (8 ms per second)
questions.explanation: Processes: 4,000 × 25 µs = 100 ms per second (10 %); threads: 4,000 × 5 µs = 20 ms (2 %); saving = 80 ms per second = 8 %.

questions.questionText: An RTOS application has 8 tasks, each with a TCB of 96 bytes and a stack of 1 KB (1 KB = 1024 bytes). How much RAM do the TCBs and stacks need in total?
options: 8960 bytes
8768 bytes
8288 bytes
8192 bytes
questions.explanation: 8 × (96 + 1024) = 8 × 1120 = 8960 bytes. 8768 uses 1 KB = 1000 bytes, 8288 counts only one TCB and 8192 counts only the stacks.

questions.questionText: After the kernel's own data, 20 KB of RAM (1 KB = 1024 bytes) remains for tasks. Each task needs an 88-byte TCB and a 1.5 KB stack. How many tasks can be created?
questions.explanation: Per task 88 + 1536 = 1624 bytes, and 20,480 / 1624 = 12.6, so only 12 complete tasks fit. 13 ignores the TCBs (20,480 / 1536 = 13.3), 14 rounds 13.3 up and 232 ignores the stacks.

questions.questionText: An external event raises an interrupt. The interrupt latency is 5 µs, the ISR runs for 20 µs and makes a waiting high-priority task ready, the scheduler then takes 3 µs and the context switch 4 µs. How long after the interrupt request does the task start executing?
options: 25 µs
29 µs
32 µs
12 µs
questions.explanation: t = latency + ISR + scheduler + switch = 5 + 20 + 3 + 4 = 32 µs. 25 µs stops at the end of the ISR, 29 µs forgets the scheduler and 12 µs forgets the ISR.

questions.questionText: On an MCU at 16 MHz the hardware needs 48 clock cycles to recognise an interrupt and enter its ISR. The kernel's longest section with interrupts disabled lasts 15 µs, and the ISR runs for 10 µs. What is the worst-case time from the interrupt request to the completion of the ISR?
options: 28 µs
13 µs
25 µs
18 µs
questions.explanation: Hardware entry = 48 / 16 MHz = 3 µs; worst case = 15 (interrupts disabled) + 3 + 10 = 28 µs. 13 µs ignores the critical section, 25 µs ignores the entry cycles and 18 µs is the latency without the ISR.

questions.questionText: In FreeRTOS with a 1 ms system tick, the highest-priority task in the system calls vTaskDelay(10) at an arbitrary moment between two ticks. How long does it actually stay blocked?
options: Between 9 ms and 10 ms
Exactly 10 ms
Between 10 ms and 11 ms
Between 0 ms and 10 ms
questions.explanation: The task unblocks at the 10th tick interrupt after the call, and the first of those ticks arrives less than one full period after the call, so the real delay is between 9 and 10 tick periods. Because it is the highest-priority task it runs as soon as it becomes ready.

questions.questionText: An RTOS keeps a 32-bit unsigned tick counter incremented by a 10 kHz tick. After how long does the counter wrap around to zero?
options: 4.97 days
49.7 days
2.49 days
119.3 days
questions.explanation: 2^32 / 10,000 Hz = 429,497 s, and 429,497 / 86,400 = 4.97 days. 49.7 days is the 1 kHz figure, 2.49 days treats the counter as signed and 119.3 is the number of hours, not days.

questions.questionText: An RTOS keeps a 32-bit ready bitmap in which bit i is 1 when a task of priority i is ready, and a larger number means a higher priority. The bitmap is 00A4 0010H. Which priority is dispatched, and how is it found in constant time?
options: Priority 4, found as the lowest set bit
Priority 21, found as 31 − CLZ(bitmap)
Priority 23, found as 31 − CLZ(bitmap)
Priority 8, found as CLZ(bitmap)
questions.explanation: 00A4 0010H has bits 23, 21, 18 and 4 set; count-leading-zeros gives 8, so the highest set bit is 31 − 8 = 23. The lowest set bit would be the lowest priority, and 8 is the CLZ value itself.

questions.questionText: Which design choice increases an RTOS's worst-case interrupt latency?
options: Keeping ISRs short and deferring the remaining work to a task
Disabling interrupts for long critical sections inside the kernel or drivers
Allowing nested interrupts with hardware priorities
Placing the interrupt vector table in fast on-chip memory
questions.explanation: An interrupt that arrives while interrupts are disabled must wait until they are re-enabled, so the longest disabled section adds directly to the worst-case latency. The other choices reduce latency.

questions.questionText: Which statement about an RTOS is NOT correct?
options: An RTOS always delivers higher average throughput than a general-purpose OS on the same hardware
It uses priority-based pre-emptive scheduling so that urgent tasks run promptly
It specifies worst-case times for its services and interrupt handling
It is usually small enough to run from on-chip Flash with little RAM
questions.explanation: An RTOS optimises predictability, not average throughput; a GPOS is often faster on average. The other three statements are standard RTOS characteristics.

questions.questionText: Which system is best described as soft real-time?
options: An audio streaming player, where a late sample causes a brief glitch but playback continues
An anti-lock braking controller
A cardiac pacemaker
A fly-by-wire flight control computer
questions.explanation: In a soft real-time system a missed deadline only degrades quality, and the late result still has some value. Braking, pacing and flight control are hard real-time: a miss can be catastrophic.

questions.questionText: A system discards any result that arrives after its deadline because it is then useless, but it tolerates occasional misses without failing. This is:
options: A hard real-time system
A soft real-time system
A non-real-time batch system
A firm real-time system
questions.explanation: Firm real-time: a late result has zero value and is dropped, yet infrequent misses are acceptable. Hard real-time cannot tolerate any miss, and in soft real-time late results keep some value.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of multithreading within one process?
options: The application stays responsive while one thread waits for I/O
Threads are protected from each other's memory errors because each has a private address space
Threads can share data directly, without kernel IPC
Creating and switching threads is cheaper than creating and switching processes
questions.explanation: Threads of a process share one address space, so a stray pointer in one thread can corrupt the others; protection is a property of separate processes. The other three are the classic benefits of threads.

questions.questionText: In the many-to-one threading model, many user-level threads are mapped onto one kernel thread. What happens when one of them makes a blocking system call?
options: The whole process blocks, because the kernel sees only one schedulable thread
Only that thread blocks, and the kernel schedules another thread of the process
The kernel automatically turns the call into a non-blocking one
The other threads carry on in parallel on other CPU cores
questions.explanation: The kernel is unaware of user-level threads, so blocking its single kernel thread stops them all; this, and the lack of multicore parallelism, is why most systems use the one-to-one model.

questions.questionText: Two RTOS tasks call the same C function, and either may be pre-empted inside it. Which version is reentrant?
options: int f(int x) { static int t; t = x * 2; return t + 1; }
int f(int x) { int t = x * 2; return t + 1; }
int t; int f(int x) { t = x * 2; return t + 1; }
int f(int x) { static int n = 0; n++; return x * n; }
questions.explanation: A reentrant function keeps its working data in locals on the caller's stack, so each task has its own copy. The static and global variables in the other versions are shared, so a pre-empting task can overwrite them mid-calculation.

questions.questionText: A super-loop (foreground/background) program calls A(), B() and C() in turn; they take 2 ms, 5 ms and 3 ms. A checks an event flag as its first action. In the worst case, how long after the flag is set does A next check it?
options: 8 ms
5 ms
10 ms
2 ms
questions.explanation: In the worst case the flag is set just after A has checked it, so the next check comes one full loop later: 2 + 5 + 3 = 10 ms. 8 ms leaves out A's own run time; a pre-emptive RTOS would instead respond within its bounded latency.

questions.questionText: How does a user-mode application normally obtain a kernel service such as reading a file?
options: It executes a system call, a trap instruction that switches the CPU to kernel mode at a fixed entry point
It jumps directly to the kernel function's address while staying in user mode
It disables interrupts and programs the disk controller registers itself
It reads the kernel's memory directly through a pointer
questions.explanation: User mode cannot execute privileged instructions or touch kernel memory, so the application traps into the kernel through a controlled entry point, and the kernel returns the result.

questions.questionText: In RTOS timing, what is the time from the moment an ISR makes a high-priority task ready until that task starts running called?
options: Scheduling (dispatch) latency
Interrupt latency
Task execution time
Tick period
questions.explanation: Interrupt latency ends when the ISR starts; the scheduling or dispatch latency covers the scheduler decision and the context switch that follow the ISR.

questions.questionText: What is the system tick in an RTOS?
options: The oscillator that clocks the CPU pipeline
A periodic timer interrupt the kernel uses to count time for delays, timeouts and time slicing
The instruction that ends a task
A counter of how many tasks are ready
questions.explanation: A hardware timer interrupts at a fixed rate, typically 100 Hz to 1 kHz; the tick handler advances the kernel's time, wakes tasks whose delays expire and rotates equal-priority tasks.

questions.questionText: Many microcontroller RTOSes, such as FreeRTOS on a Cortex-M microcontroller, run all tasks in one address space without an MMU. What is the main consequence?
options: Tasks cannot share global variables at all
Every context switch must copy the whole task image into RAM
A stray pointer in one task can corrupt another task's data or the kernel, unless an MPU is used to restrict access
Tasks must be written in assembly language
questions.explanation: Without memory protection nothing stops a task writing anywhere in RAM; an optional memory protection unit (MPU) can confine each task to its own regions.

questions.questionText: In a cooperative (non-pre-emptive) kernel, when does a running task give up the CPU?
options: Whenever a higher-priority task becomes ready
Only when it blocks, yields or finishes
At every system tick
Whenever any interrupt occurs
questions.explanation: Without pre-emption the kernel switches tasks only at points the running task chooses; an interrupt runs its ISR and then returns to the same task. Pre-emption on readiness or on the tick describes a pre-emptive kernel.

subtopics.title: Multitasking & Task Scheduling
subtopics.subtitle: Multitasking models, FCFS, SJF, RR, priority, rate-monotonic, EDF and priority inversion

concepts.text: Multiprogramming, Multitasking and Multiprocessing

rows: Several programs in memory; CPU switches when one waits for I/O
CPU rapidly switched among tasks so they appear concurrent
Tasks run truly in parallel on two or more processors/cores
Several threads of one process scheduled concurrently

concepts.text: In cooperative (non-pre-emptive) multitasking a task keeps the CPU until it voluntarily yields or blocks, so one misbehaving task can starve all others and response time depends on the longest task. In pre-emptive multitasking the kernel can take the CPU away at a tick or when a higher-priority task becomes ready, giving bounded response for high-priority work. Most RTOSes use priority-based pre-emptive scheduling, often with round robin among equal-priority tasks.
Scheduler, dispatcher and scheduling criteria:
items: Scheduler: decides which ready task runs next according to the policy.
Dispatcher: performs the context switch and jumps to the chosen task; its delay is dispatch latency.
Maximise CPU utilisation and throughput (tasks completed per unit time).
Minimise turnaround time, waiting time and response time.
Real-time criterion: meet every deadline (predictability over average performance).

concepts.text: Scheduling Algorithms

rows: Simple; convoy effect behind long jobs
Minimum average waiting time; may starve long jobs
Fixed time quantum in circular order
Fair; quantum too small raises switch overhead
Fixed priority: shorter period = higher priority

concepts.text: FCFS worked example: bursts P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3 ms arriving in that order give waiting times 0, 24 and 27 ms, an average of 17 ms. If the short jobs arrive first (P2, P3, P1) the waits become 0, 3 and 6 ms, average 3 ms; this gap is the convoy effect. SJF always picks the order that minimises average waiting time, e.g. bursts 6, 8, 7, 3 run as 3, 6, 7, 8 giving waits 0, 3, 9, 16 and an average of 7 ms.

Round robin worked example with quantum q = 4 ms on the same bursts 24, 3, 3: P1 runs 0 to 4, P2 4 to 7, P3 7 to 10, then P1 finishes 10 to 30. Waiting times are P1 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7 ms, average about 5.67 ms. A very large quantum turns RR into FCFS; a very small one wastes CPU on context switches.
Rate-Monotonic and Earliest Deadline First

concepts.plainText: U = sum(C_i/T_i) <= n(2^(1/n) - 1); tends to ln 2 = 0.693 as n grows

concepts.text: RMS check for three periodic tasks (C, T) = (1, 4), (2, 6) and (1, 10) ms: U = 0.25 + 0.333 + 0.10 = 0.683. The Liu and Layland bound for n = 3 is 3(2^(1/3) - 1) = 0.780. Since 0.683 <= 0.780 the set is guaranteed schedulable under RMS, with priorities T = 4 highest and T = 10 lowest. If U lies between the bound and 1 the test is inconclusive and response-time analysis is needed.

concepts.plainText: EDF: schedulable if U = sum(C_i/T_i) <= 1 (deadline = period)

concepts.text: Priority Inversion

Priority inversion occurs when a high-priority task H blocks on a resource (mutex) held by a low-priority task L, and a medium-priority task M, which does not need the resource, pre-empts L. H is then effectively delayed by M for an unbounded time. A famous case is the 1997 Mars Pathfinder resets, fixed by enabling priority inheritance on a mutex.
Remedies for priority inversion:
items: Priority inheritance: L temporarily inherits H's priority while holding the resource, so M cannot pre-empt it.
Priority ceiling protocol: each resource has a ceiling equal to the highest priority of any task using it; a task locking it runs at the ceiling, which also prevents deadlock between such resources.
Keep critical sections short and avoid sharing resources across widely different priorities.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Scheduling Calculations and Schedulability

Every scheduling calculation starts from a Gantt chart and then uses four measures per task: completion time CT, turnaround time TAT = CT - arrival time, waiting time WT = TAT - CPU burst, and response time = first start - arrival time. State the tie-break rule (usually earlier arrival, then lower index) and, for round robin, where a new arrival joins the queue; the usual textbook convention is that a task arriving at the same instant a quantum expires is queued ahead of the pre-empted task. A pre-emptive policy is re-evaluated at every arrival and completion, a non-pre-emptive one only when the running task finishes or blocks.

Worked example 1: SRTF (pre-emptive SJF), no I/O, times in ms
Task  Arrival  Burst
P1    0        8
P2    1        4
P3    2        9
P4    3        5
Gantt: | P1 0-1 | P2 1-5 | P4 5-10 | P1 10-17 | P3 17-26 |
t = 1: P2 (4) is shorter than P1's remaining 7, so P1 is pre-empted
WT = CT - AT - burst: P1 17-0-8 = 9    P2 5-1-4 = 0
                      P3 26-2-9 = 15   P4 10-3-5 = 2
Average WT = 26/4 = 6.5 ms (non-pre-emptive SJF gives 7.75 ms)

concepts.plainText: R_i = C_i + B_i + sum over higher-priority tasks j of ceil(R_i / T_j) x C_j; iterate from R_i = C_i + B_i

concepts.text: The Liu and Layland bound comes from the critical instant: a task's worst response occurs when it is released together with every higher-priority task, and n(2^(1/n) - 1) is the least upper bound: every set at or below it is schedulable, while just above it some unlucky choice of periods and execution times misses a deadline. The bound is sufficient but not necessary; for example, task sets with harmonic periods (each period divides the next) stay RM-schedulable right up to U = 1. Response-time analysis (RTA) is exact for fixed priorities with D <= T: start with R = C + B, recompute the interference from higher-priority tasks until the value stops changing, and the task is schedulable if that R <= D. B is the blocking caused by lower-priority tasks holding shared resources.

Worked example 2: T1 (C=1, T=3), T2 (C=3, T=8), T3 (C=3, T=12), D = T
U = 1/3 + 3/8 + 3/12 = 0.958 > 3(2^(1/3) - 1) = 0.780 -> RM bound inconclusive
RTA with RM priorities T1 > T2 > T3:
 R1 = 1 <= 3  ok
 R2: 3 -> 3 + ceil(3/3)x1 = 4 -> 3 + ceil(4/3)x1 = 5 -> 5  <= 8  ok
 R3 = 3 + ceil(R/3)x1 + ceil(R/8)x3:
      3 -> 7 -> 9 -> 12 -> 13 > 12  -> T3 misses under RM
EDF: U = 0.958 <= 1 -> schedulable; T3's first job ends at t = 9 (deadline 12)

rows: RTA; the bound n(2^(1/n) - 1) is only sufficient
All pre-emptive policies on one CPU
Dynamic: smaller laxity d - t - c = higher
All pre-emptive policies on one CPU
U <= 1 when D = T, but far more context switches

concepts.text: How long priority inversion lasts depends on the locking protocol. With no protocol, a high-priority task H that is blocked on a mutex also waits for every medium-priority task that pre-empts the holder, so its blocking has no fixed limit. Basic priority inheritance limits H's blocking to at most one critical section of each lower-priority task that shares a resource with it, but blocking can still chain through several holders and deadlock is still possible. The priority ceiling protocol, and its simpler immediate-ceiling form used in OSEK/AUTOSAR kernels, limits blocking to a single critical section and makes deadlock through nested locks impossible.
Deadlines, laxity and jitter:
items: Relative deadline D is measured from a job's release; the absolute deadline is d = release time + D, so job k of a task released first at t = 0 has d = (k - 1)T + D.
Laxity (slack) at time t is d - t - remaining execution; least-laxity-first runs the job with the smallest laxity, and a negative laxity means the deadline can no longer be met.
Release jitter is the variation in when a job actually becomes ready, for example up to one tick when periodic tasks are released by a 1 ms system tick.
Response (output) jitter is the spread of response times, R_max - R_min; control loops keep it small by sampling and actuating at the start of a high-priority task or inside a timer ISR.

concepts.plainText: Laxity = absolute deadline d - current time t - remaining execution time c_rem

concepts.text: Common slips: measuring waiting time from t = 0 instead of from arrival; letting a newly arrived job cut in under a non-pre-emptive policy; using ln 2 = 0.693 instead of the bound for the actual n; calling a set unschedulable just because U exceeds the RM bound, when that test is only sufficient; and applying U <= 1 to EDF when deadlines are shorter than periods, where a processor-demand test is needed instead.

For RM questions work in this order: compute U, compare it with n(2^(1/n) - 1) for the actual n, and if U lies between the bound and 1, run response-time analysis for each task from the highest priority down. For EDF with deadlines equal to periods, the single check U <= 1 decides the answer.

formulas.plainText: RMS bound: U <= n(2^(1/n) - 1)
As n grows the RMS bound tends to ln 2 = 0.693
EDF schedulability: U <= 1
Average waiting time = sum of waiting times / n

notes.text: Memorise RMS bounds: n = 1 gives 1.0, n = 2 gives 0.828, n = 3 gives 0.780, n = 4 gives 0.757, and the limit is 0.693.
The RMS bound is sufficient, not necessary: a task set with U above n(2^(1/n) - 1) but at most 1 may still be schedulable. U > 1 is never schedulable on one processor.
RMS is static (priorities fixed at design time from periods); EDF is dynamic (priorities change with each job's absolute deadline) and can use up to 100% of the CPU.

formulas.title: RMS utilisation bound
formulas.description: Sufficient test for schedulability of n independent periodic tasks under rate-monotonic scheduling.

formulas.title: EDF utilisation test
formulas.plainText: U = sum(C_i/T_i) <= 1
formulas.description: Necessary and sufficient test for pre-emptive EDF when deadlines equal periods.

formulas.title: RMS asymptotic bound
formulas.plainText: Limit of RMS bound = ln 2 = 0.693
formulas.description: Any number of tasks with total utilisation at most 69.3% is RMS-schedulable.

formulas.title: Average waiting time
formulas.plainText: Average waiting time = sum of waits / n
formulas.description: Common figure of merit used to compare FCFS, SJF, RR and priority schedules.

flashcards.back: Cooperative tasks run until they yield voluntarily; pre-emptive kernels can interrupt a task at a tick or when a higher-priority task becomes ready.

flashcards.front: What is the RMS utilisation bound for 2 tasks?
What is priority inversion and how is it fixed?
flashcards.back: A high-priority task waits on a resource held by a low-priority task that is pre-empted by a medium-priority task; fixed by priority inheritance or priority ceiling.

flashcards.front: Which scheduling algorithm gives the minimum average waiting time?
flashcards.back: Shortest Job First (SJF), or its pre-emptive form SRTF, for a given set of known burst times.

questions.questionText: What is the Liu and Layland rate-monotonic utilisation bound for three periodic tasks?
questions.explanation: n(2^(1/n) - 1) with n = 3 gives 3(1.2599 - 1) = 0.780. 0.828 is for n = 2, 0.757 for n = 4 and 0.693 is the limit.

questions.questionText: Four processes arrive at time 0 with CPU bursts 6, 8, 7 and 3 ms. What is the average waiting time under non-pre-emptive SJF?
options: 7 ms
6 ms
8 ms
questions.explanation: SJF order is 3, 6, 7, 8 giving waits 0, 3, 9 and 16 ms; the average is 28/4 = 7 ms.

questions.questionText: A high-priority task is blocked on a mutex held by a low-priority task, while a medium-priority task keeps pre-empting the low-priority one. This problem is called:
options: Deadlock
Starvation by ageing
Thrashing
Priority inversion
questions.explanation: The high-priority task is effectively delayed by a lower-priority one; this is priority inversion, solved by priority inheritance or priority ceiling.

questions.questionText: Which is an advantage of cooperative multitasking compared with pre-emptive multitasking?
options: A high-priority task always starts within one tick of becoming ready
A task that never yields cannot delay the other tasks
Every deadline is met whenever total utilisation is at most 1
Task switches happen only where the programmer yields, so data shared between tasks needs less locking
questions.explanation: Because a cooperative task is never interrupted by another task between its yield points, a sequence of accesses to shared data between two yields is automatically indivisible with respect to other tasks (ISRs still need care). The price is that response time depends on the longest code between yields.

questions.questionText: Why do hard real-time systems normally use pre-emptive priority scheduling instead of cooperative scheduling?
options: A high-priority task's response time no longer depends on how long lower-priority tasks run before yielding
Pre-emptive scheduling removes the need for semaphores and mutexes
Pre-emptive scheduling always gives higher throughput than cooperative scheduling
Pre-emptive scheduling performs no context switches, so it has no overhead
questions.explanation: With pre-emption the kernel switches to a higher-priority task as soon as it becomes ready, so its response is bounded by kernel latency rather than by the longest code between yields. Pre-emption actually adds context switches and makes shared-data protection more important.

questions.questionText: A priority-based pre-emptive RTOS has time slicing enabled. Tasks A and B are ready at the same, highest priority, and a lower-priority task C is also ready. How is the CPU shared?
options: A and B alternate, one time slice each, and C runs only when neither A nor B is ready
A runs until it blocks or finishes, and only then does B run
A, B and C share the CPU in round-robin order, one slice each
C runs every third slice so that it does not starve
questions.explanation: Round robin applies only among tasks of the highest ready priority; a lower-priority task gets the CPU only when no higher-priority task is ready, so C may starve if A and B never block.

questions.questionText: A cooperative kernel always picks the highest-priority ready task whenever the running task yields. Three background tasks run for at most 3 ms, 6 ms and 11 ms between yields. An urgent task U with the highest priority becomes ready at an arbitrary moment. Ignoring kernel overhead, what is U's worst-case delay before it starts?
options: 20 ms, the sum of the three runs
Just under 11 ms, the longest run between yields of any other task
6.67 ms, the average run length
Zero, because U has the highest priority
questions.explanation: U may become ready just after the 11 ms task has started, and nothing can pre-empt it, so U waits almost 11 ms; when that task yields, the scheduler picks U first, so the other tasks add nothing.

questions.questionText: Which practical difficulty limits the use of pure shortest-job-first (SJF) scheduling?
options: It gives the highest average waiting time of all the common algorithms
It cannot be used when processes arrive at different times
It needs a separate hardware timer for every process
The length of each process's next CPU burst is not known in advance and has to be predicted
questions.explanation: SJF minimises average waiting time, but only if burst lengths are known; real schedulers estimate them, for example by exponential averaging of past bursts.

questions.questionText: Which scheduling criterion does a CPU scheduler try to MAXIMISE rather than minimise?
options: Throughput
Waiting time
Turnaround time
Response time
questions.explanation: Throughput (jobs completed per unit time) and CPU utilisation are maximised; waiting, turnaround and response times are minimised.

questions.questionText: Several short processes wait behind one long CPU-bound process, so the average waiting time becomes large. This convoy effect is characteristic of which algorithm?
options: First-come, first-served (FCFS)
Round robin
Shortest remaining time first (SRTF)
Earliest deadline first (EDF)
questions.explanation: FCFS is non-pre-emptive and ignores burst length, so short jobs queued behind a long one all wait for it to finish.

questions.questionText: Which of these scheduling algorithms is inherently non-pre-emptive?
options: Round robin
Shortest remaining time first (SRTF)
First-come, first-served (FCFS)
Earliest deadline first (EDF) as used in RTOS kernels
questions.explanation: FCFS runs each job to completion (or until it blocks) in arrival order; round robin pre-empts at the end of each quantum, and SRTF and EDF pre-empt when a more urgent job arrives.

questions.questionText: Jobs J1, J2 and J3 arrive at time 0 in that order with CPU bursts of 10 ms, 4 ms and 6 ms and are scheduled FCFS. What is the turnaround time of J3?
options: 20 ms
14 ms
6 ms
questions.explanation: J3 starts after 10 + 4 = 14 ms and completes at 20 ms, so its turnaround = 20 - 0 = 20 ms (14 ms is its waiting time and 14.67 ms is the average turnaround).

questions.questionText: Processes P1, P2, P3 and P4 arrive at 0, 1, 2 and 3 ms with CPU bursts of 5, 3, 8 and 6 ms and are scheduled FCFS (no I/O). What is the average waiting time?
questions.explanation: Gantt: P1 0-5, P2 5-8, P3 8-16, P4 16-22. Waiting = start - arrival = 0, 4, 6 and 13 ms, so the average is 23/4 = 5.75 ms.

questions.questionText: Non-pre-emptive SJF schedules P1, P2, P3 and P4, which arrive at 0, 1, 2 and 3 ms with CPU bursts of 8, 4, 2 and 1 ms. What is the average waiting time?
options: 7 ms
5.5 ms
questions.explanation: Only P1 is present at t = 0, so it runs 0-8; then the shortest waiting job goes first: P4 8-9, P3 9-11, P2 11-15. Waits are 0, 10, 7 and 5 ms, average 22/4 = 5.5 ms.

questions.questionText: Under SRTF (pre-emptive SJF), P1, P2, P3 and P4 arrive at 0, 1, 2 and 4 ms with CPU bursts of 7, 5, 2 and 3 ms. What is the average waiting time?
options: 5.5 ms
6.5 ms
questions.explanation: Gantt: P1 0-1, P2 1-2, P3 2-4, P4 4-7, P2 7-11, P1 11-17. Waiting = CT - arrival - burst = 10, 5, 0 and 0 ms, average 15/4 = 3.75 ms.

questions.questionText: Under SRTF, P1, P2, P3 and P4 arrive at 0, 2, 3 and 5 ms with CPU bursts of 9, 4, 6 and 2 ms. What is the total waiting time of P1?
options: 14 ms
21 ms
12 ms
4.5 ms

questions.questionText: In priority scheduling, a low-priority process may never run because higher-priority processes keep arriving. Which technique prevents this?
options: Increasing the time quantum
Ageing: gradually raising the priority of processes that have waited a long time
Priority inversion
Running the highest-priority process with interrupts disabled
questions.explanation: The problem is starvation (indefinite blocking); ageing raises a waiting process's priority over time so that it eventually runs.

questions.questionText: Non-pre-emptive priority scheduling (smaller number = higher priority) is applied to P1 (arrival 0 ms, burst 4 ms, priority 3), P2 (1, 3, 1), P3 (2, 5, 4) and P4 (3, 2, 2). What is the average waiting time?
options: 3.5 ms
5 ms
7 ms
questions.explanation: P1 runs 0-4 because it is alone at t = 0; then P2 4-7, P4 7-9 and P3 9-14. Waits are 0, 3, 4 and 7 ms, average 14/4 = 3.5 ms.

questions.questionText: Pre-emptive priority scheduling (smaller number = higher priority) runs P1 (arrival 0 ms, burst 2 ms, priority 4), P2 (1, 2, 1), P3 (3, 2, 3) and P4 (4, 4, 2). What is the average turnaround time?
options: 4 ms
5.5 ms
3 ms
7.5 ms
questions.explanation: Gantt: P1 0-1, P2 1-3, P3 3-4, P4 4-8, P3 8-9, P1 9-10. Turnaround = CT - arrival = 10, 2, 6 and 4 ms, average 22/4 = 5.5 ms.

questions.questionText: What happens to round-robin scheduling if the time quantum is made longer than the longest CPU burst of every process?
options: It behaves like SJF
Context-switch overhead rises sharply
It behaves like FCFS
It becomes rate-monotonic scheduling
questions.explanation: No process is ever pre-empted by the quantum, so each runs to completion in queue order, which is exactly FCFS; overhead falls rather than rises.

questions.questionText: Three processes arrive at time 0 in the order P1, P2, P3 with CPU bursts of 10, 4 and 7 ms. Round robin with a 3 ms quantum is used and context-switch time is ignored. What is the average waiting time?
options: 8 ms
9 ms
3 ms
11 ms
questions.explanation: Gantt: P1 0-3, P2 3-6, P3 6-9, P1 9-12, P2 12-13, P3 13-16, P1 16-19, P3 19-20, P1 20-21. Completions 21, 13 and 20 ms give waits 11, 9 and 13 ms, average 33/3 = 11 ms.

questions.questionText: Round robin with a 2 ms quantum schedules P1, P2, P3 and P4, arriving at 0, 1, 2 and 3 ms with CPU bursts of 5, 3, 1 and 2 ms. A process arriving at the same instant a quantum expires joins the ready queue ahead of the pre-empted process. What is the average waiting time?
options: 5 ms
4.5 ms
questions.explanation: Gantt: P1 0-2, P2 2-4, P3 4-5, P1 5-7, P4 7-9, P2 9-10, P1 10-11. Waiting = CT - arrival - burst = 6, 6, 2 and 4 ms, average 18/4 = 4.5 ms.

questions.questionText: Under round robin with a 4 ms quantum, a process needs 17 ms of CPU time, never blocks and shares the CPU with other CPU-bound processes. How many times is it pre-empted by quantum expiry before it finishes?
questions.explanation: It receives ceil(17/4) = 5 quanta (4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 1 ms); it is pre-empted at the end of the first four and finishes during the fifth.

questions.questionText: An SJF scheduler predicts the next CPU burst with exponential averaging, τ(n+1) = α·t(n) + (1 - α)·τ(n), where α = 0.5 and the initial guess τ(1) = 10 ms. The next two measured bursts are t(1) = 6 ms and t(2) = 4 ms. What is the predicted burst τ(3)?
options: 8 ms
5 ms
6 ms

questions.questionText: FCFS runs P1 (arrival 0 ms, burst 3 ms), P2 (arrival 5 ms, burst 4 ms) and P3 (arrival 6 ms, burst 2 ms). Over the interval from 0 until the last process finishes, what are the CPU utilisation and the throughput?
options: 100 % and 0.273 processes per ms
81.8 % and 0.333 processes per ms
81.8 % and 0.273 processes per ms
18.2 % and 0.273 processes per ms
questions.explanation: P1 runs 0-3, the CPU is idle 3-5, P2 runs 5-9 and P3 9-11. Utilisation = 9/11 = 81.8 % and throughput = 3 processes / 11 ms = 0.273 per ms.

questions.questionText: Which scheduling algorithm assigns priorities dynamically, according to each job's absolute deadline?
options: Rate-monotonic scheduling (RMS)
Earliest deadline first (EDF)
Deadline-monotonic scheduling (DMS)
First-come, first-served (FCFS)
questions.explanation: EDF gives the highest priority to the ready job whose absolute deadline is nearest, so priorities change at run time; RMS and DMS fix priorities at design time.

questions.questionText: Three periodic tasks have (C, T) = (1, 5), (2, 10) and (3, 20) ms. What is their total processor utilisation?

Four independent periodic tasks with deadlines equal to periods have (C, T) = (2, 8), (2, 10), (3, 20) and (6, 40) ms. What does the Liu and Layland test say about rate-monotonic scheduling of this set?
options: U = 0.75 exceeds ln 2 = 0.693, so RM will miss a deadline
U = 0.75 is above the bound 0.743, so the test is inconclusive
U = 0.75 <= 0.757, so the set is guaranteed schedulable
The test cannot be applied because the periods are not harmonic
questions.explanation: U = 0.25 + 0.20 + 0.15 + 0.15 = 0.75 and the bound for n = 4 is 4(2^(1/4) - 1) = 0.757, so all deadlines are met; 0.693 is only the limit for very large n.

questions.questionText: Tasks (C, T) = (1, 4), (2, 6) and (3, 10) ms, with deadlines equal to periods, share one processor. Which conclusion follows from the utilisation tests alone?
options: The RM bound test is inconclusive (U = 0.883 > 0.780), but EDF is guaranteed to meet every deadline (U <= 1)
RM is guaranteed to meet every deadline because U = 0.883 <= 1
No algorithm can schedule the set because U exceeds 0.780
EDF cannot be used because the periods are not harmonic
questions.explanation: U = 0.25 + 0.333 + 0.30 = 0.883, above the n = 3 bound 0.780 but not above 1. (Response-time analysis shows RM does in fact meet every deadline here, with R3 = 10 ms, but the utilisation test alone cannot tell.)

questions.questionText: Under pre-emptive RM, T1 (C = 2 ms, T = 4 ms) and T2 (C = 3 ms, T = 10 ms) are both released at t = 0. At what time does the first job of T2 complete?
options: 5 ms
7 ms
3 ms
10 ms
questions.explanation: T1 0-2, T2 2-4, T1's second job pre-empts at 4 and runs 4-6, then T2 finishes its last 1 ms at 6-7, well before its deadline of 10 ms.

questions.questionText: Using response-time analysis, what is the worst-case response time of T3 under RM for T1 (C = 2, T = 5), T2 (C = 2, T = 8) and T3 (C = 3, T = 20), all in ms with deadlines equal to periods?
options: 13 ms
7 ms
11 ms
20 ms
questions.explanation: R = 3 + 2 x ceil(R/5) + 2 x ceil(R/8) iterates 3 -> 7 -> 9 -> 11 -> 13 -> 13, so R3 = 13 ms, within its 20 ms deadline.

questions.questionText: T1 (C = 2 ms, T = 5 ms) and T2 (C = 4 ms, T = 7 ms), with deadlines equal to periods, are released together at t = 0 and scheduled by pre-emptive RM. What happens to the first job of T2?
options: It completes at t = 6 and meets its deadline
It still needs 1 ms at t = 7 and misses its deadline
It completes at t = 7, exactly at its deadline
It still needs 2 ms at t = 7 and misses its deadline
questions.explanation: T1 runs 0-2, T2 2-5 (3 ms done), then T1's second job pre-empts it at 5-7, so T2 has 1 ms left at its deadline. Check: U = 0.971 > 0.828 and RTA gives 4 -> 6 -> 8 > 7. (EDF would finish it at t = 6.)

questions.questionText: Pre-emptive EDF schedules T1 (C = 1, T = 3), T2 (C = 2, T = 6) and T3 (C = 3, T = 10), all in ms with deadlines equal to periods and all released at t = 0. At what time does the first job of T3 complete?
options: 8 ms
7 ms
10 ms
It misses its deadline at 10 ms
questions.explanation: T1 0-1, T2 1-3, T1 3-4, T3 4-6, T1 6-7 (deadline 9), then T3 7-8 because its deadline 10 is earlier than the 12 ms deadline of T2's second job. Under RM, T2 would run 7-9 instead and T3 would miss at 10 ms.

questions.questionText: Tasks (C, T) = (1, 4) and (2, 10) ms already run on a processor. A third task with a 20 ms period (deadline = period) is added. What is the largest whole-millisecond execution time C3 that is guaranteed schedulable (a) by the Liu and Layland RM utilisation bound and (b) under EDF?
options: 7 ms by the RM bound and 11 ms under EDF
6 ms by the RM bound and 11 ms under EDF
4 ms by the RM bound and 11 ms under EDF
6 ms by the RM bound and 20 ms under EDF

questions.questionText: Periodic tasks with periods 4, 6 and 10 ms are all released at t = 0. What is the hyperperiod, and how many jobs are released in one hyperperiod?
options: 240 ms and 124 jobs
60 ms and 3 jobs
60 ms and 31 jobs
20 ms and 3 jobs

questions.questionText: Tasks (C, T) = (2, 4), (2, 8) and (4, 16) ms with deadlines equal to periods have total utilisation 1.0. Are they schedulable under pre-emptive RM?
options: Yes; the periods are harmonic, so RM can use 100 % of the CPU, and every deadline in the 16 ms hyperperiod is met
No; U = 1.0 exceeds the n = 3 bound of 0.780
Only under EDF, because RM can never exceed 69.3 % utilisation
No; T3 misses its deadline at t = 16 ms
questions.explanation: Timeline: T1 0-2, T2 2-4, T1 4-6, T3 6-8, T1 8-10, T2 10-12, T1 12-14, T3 14-16, so every job meets its deadline (RTA gives R3 = 16 ms = D). The Liu and Layland bound is only a sufficient test.

questions.questionText: Independent periodic tasks have relative deadlines shorter than their periods (D < T). Which fixed-priority assignment is optimal for them?
options: Rate-monotonic: the shorter the period, the higher the priority
Longest execution time first
Priority in order of first release time
Deadline-monotonic: the shorter the relative deadline, the higher the priority
questions.explanation: Leung and Whitehead showed deadline-monotonic assignment is optimal among fixed-priority schemes when D <= T; RM is the special case D = T.

questions.questionText: Which statement about pre-emptive EDF scheduling on one processor is NOT correct?
options: Priorities are decided at run time from each job's absolute deadline
With deadlines equal to periods, a task set is schedulable if and only if U <= 1
EDF priorities are fixed at design time from the task periods
EDF can schedule some task sets that rate-monotonic scheduling cannot
questions.explanation: EDF is a dynamic-priority policy: the job with the nearest absolute deadline runs, so relative priorities of tasks change over time. Fixed priorities from periods describe RM.

questions.questionText: A transient overload briefly pushes processor demand above 100 %. How do RM and EDF typically behave?
options: Under EDF the lowest-priority tasks miss first; under RM misses cascade through all tasks
Both drop only the task with the longest period
EDF automatically discards the least important task, so no deadlines are missed
Under RM the lowest-priority tasks miss first while high-priority tasks stay protected; under EDF misses are hard to predict and can cascade
questions.explanation: RM's fixed priorities shield the high-priority (short-period) tasks during overload, whereas EDF gives priority to whichever job is nearest its deadline, so one late job can make many others late (the domino effect).

questions.questionText: Liu and Layland proved that, under fixed-priority scheduling, a task's worst-case response time occurs when it is released:
options: Just after all higher-priority tasks have completed
When the processor is otherwise idle
At the same instant as all higher-priority tasks (the critical instant)
Only at the start of the hyperperiod, and only if the periods are harmonic
questions.explanation: Releasing a task together with every higher-priority task produces the maximum interference, so testing that critical instant is enough; response-time analysis is built on the same idea.

questions.questionText: At t = 30 ms three jobs are ready: J1 (absolute deadline 50 ms, 12 ms of execution left), J2 (deadline 45 ms, 4 ms left) and J3 (deadline 48 ms, 9 ms left). Which job runs under least-laxity-first (LLF), and which under EDF?
options: Both LLF and EDF run J2
LLF runs J3 and EDF runs J2
Both LLF and EDF run J1
LLF runs J1 and EDF runs J2
questions.explanation: Laxity = d - t - remaining: J1 = 50 - 30 - 12 = 8, J2 = 11 and J3 = 9 ms, so LLF picks J1; EDF picks the earliest deadline, J2 at 45 ms.

questions.questionText: A periodic task has period 20 ms and relative deadline 15 ms, and its first job is released at t = 0. What is the absolute deadline of its third job?
options: 55 ms
60 ms
35 ms
45 ms
questions.explanation: The third job is released at 2 x 20 = 40 ms, so its absolute deadline is 40 + 15 = 55 ms.

questions.questionText: What is the main drawback of making the round-robin time quantum very small?
options: Round robin turns into FCFS
Short processes starve
Context-switch overhead takes a large share of CPU time
Average response time becomes very long
questions.explanation: Each quantum ends in a context switch, so a tiny quantum means most CPU time goes on switching; a very large quantum makes RR behave like FCFS instead.

questions.questionText: A task is released at t = 0, 10, 20 and 30 ms, and its four jobs complete at 3, 14, 22 and 35 ms. Taking response-time jitter as the largest minus the smallest response time, what is it?
options: 5 ms
3 ms
3.5 ms
13 ms
questions.explanation: Response = completion - release = 3, 4, 2 and 5 ms, so jitter = 5 - 2 = 3 ms (5 ms is the spread of the intervals between completions).

questions.questionText: In a non-pre-emptive priority system, low-priority job L (execution 8 ms) starts at t = 0. High-priority job H (execution 2 ms, relative deadline 6 ms) arrives at t = 1 ms. When does H finish, and does it meet its deadline?
options: At 3 ms, meeting its deadline
At 9 ms, missing its absolute deadline of 7 ms
At 10 ms, missing its absolute deadline of 7 ms
At 10 ms, meeting its deadline because it needs only 2 ms
questions.explanation: L cannot be pre-empted, so H waits until 8 ms and finishes at 10 ms, 3 ms after its absolute deadline 1 + 6 = 7 ms. With pre-emption it would finish at 3 ms.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the basic priority inheritance protocol is correct?
options: The blocked high-priority task lowers its own priority to that of the mutex holder
A low-priority task holding a mutex temporarily runs at the priority of the highest-priority task blocked on it, and drops back when it releases the mutex
Every task that uses the mutex runs permanently at the highest priority of any of its users
It prevents deadlock between tasks that lock two mutexes in opposite orders
questions.explanation: Inheritance is temporary and only while the holder blocks a higher-priority task; it bounds priority inversion but does not prevent deadlock.

questions.questionText: Priorities are H > M > L on a pre-emptive RTOS. L is released at 0 and immediately locks mutex X, which it holds for 3 ms of execution. H is released at 1 ms, immediately requests X and then needs 2 ms of execution while holding it. M, which never uses X, is released at 2 ms with 4 ms of execution. When does H finish without priority inheritance, and when with it?
options: 9 ms without inheritance and 7 ms with it
7 ms without inheritance and 5 ms with it
5 ms in both cases
9 ms without inheritance and 5 ms with it
questions.explanation: Without inheritance: L 0-2 (H blocks at 1), M pre-empts L 2-6, L 6-7 releases X, H 7-9. With inheritance L runs at H's priority from t = 1, M cannot pre-empt it, L releases X at 3 and H runs 3-5.

questions.questionText: Compared with basic priority inheritance, what does the priority ceiling protocol add?
options: It prevents deadlock and chained blocking, so a task is blocked by at most one lower-priority critical section
It removes the need to know in advance which tasks use each resource
It lets a task keep a mutex locked across a long sleep without delaying any other task
It allows unbounded blocking but reduces the number of context switches
questions.explanation: Each resource gets a ceiling equal to the highest priority of its users; a task may lock only when its priority is above the ceilings of resources locked by others, which rules out nested-lock deadlock and limits blocking to one critical section. This requires knowing each resource's users beforehand.

questions.questionText: High-priority task H uses mutexes R1 and R2. Lower-priority task L1 holds R1 for at most 3 ms per job, and lower-priority task L2 holds R2 for at most 5 ms per job; no critical sections are nested. Using the standard worst-case blocking bounds, what is H's maximum blocking per job under basic priority inheritance and under the priority ceiling protocol?
options: 5 ms under both protocols
8 ms under priority inheritance and 5 ms under the priority ceiling protocol
8 ms under both protocols
3 ms under priority inheritance and 8 ms under the priority ceiling protocol
questions.explanation: With inheritance H can be blocked once by each lower-priority task holding a resource it needs (chained blocking): 3 + 5 = 8 ms. The ceiling protocol allows blocking by at most one lower-priority critical section, the longest, 5 ms.

subtopics.title: Task Synchronization & Device Drivers
subtopics.subtitle: Race conditions, semaphores, mutexes, deadlock, inter-task communication and drivers

concepts.text: Race Conditions and Critical Sections

A race condition occurs when two or more tasks (or a task and an ISR) access shared data concurrently and the result depends on the timing of their execution. For example count++ compiles to load, add and store; if a task is pre-empted between load and store and another task also increments count, one update is lost. The code that touches shared data is a critical section and must execute with mutual exclusion.
Ways to protect a critical section in an embedded system:
items: Atomic operations: a single uninterruptible instruction (test-and-set, compare-and-swap, load-linked/store-conditional).
Disabling interrupts: simplest on a single core; keep it very short because it increases interrupt latency.
Scheduler lock: disables pre-emption but still allows ISRs to run.
Semaphores and mutexes: block the waiting task instead of busy-waiting.
A correct solution must give mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.

concepts.text: Semaphores and Mutexes

A semaphore (Dijkstra) is an integer counter with two atomic operations: P/wait/take decrements it and blocks the caller if no unit is available, and V/signal/give increments it and wakes a waiting task. A binary semaphore takes only 0 or 1 and is used for signalling events or simple locking. A counting semaphore is initialised to the number of identical resources (e.g. 5 buffers) and tracks how many remain.

rows: Only the locking task may unlock
Any task or ISR may give

concepts.text: Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions at once:
items: Mutual exclusion: a resource can be held by only one task.
Hold and wait: a task holds one resource while waiting for another.
No pre-emption: resources cannot be forcibly taken away.
Circular wait: a cycle of tasks each waiting for the next one's resource.
Prevention breaks one condition, e.g. always acquire locks in a fixed global order to prevent circular wait; use timeouts on takes.

concepts.text: Inter-Task Communication

rows: FIFO of fixed-size messages copied in and out; blocks when full/empty
Single latest value or pointer handover
Byte stream between writer and reader
Bit group; task waits for any or all bits
Fast bulk data; needs mutex protection

concepts.text: Device Drivers

A device driver is software that hides a peripheral's register-level details behind a standard interface (open, read, write, ioctl, close). Drivers are layered: the application calls an RTOS or OS API, which calls the device-independent driver layer, which calls the hardware-specific low-level driver or Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) that finally touches memory-mapped or port-mapped registers. Drivers also initialise the device, manage buffers and handle its interrupts.

rows: CPU repeatedly reads a status register
Device raises an interrupt when ready

concepts.text:
#define UART0_BASE  0x4000C000u
#define UART0_DR    (*(volatile uint32_t *)(UART0_BASE + 0x00))
#define UART0_FR    (*(volatile uint32_t *)(UART0_BASE + 0x18))
#define TXFF        (1u << 5)          /* transmit FIFO full */

void uart_putc(char c) {
    while (UART0_FR & TXFF) { }       /* poll status */
    UART0_DR = (uint32_t)c;           /* write data  */
}
ISR design, deferred work and reentrancy:
items: Keep ISRs short: acknowledge the device, move data to a buffer, then signal a task (semaphore/queue) to do the rest (deferred work, top half vs bottom half).
ISRs must never block, so they cannot take a mutex or wait on a queue.
volatile tells the compiler a register or ISR-shared variable can change outside program flow, so every access is really performed.
A reentrant function can be safely interrupted and called again: it uses only local variables/parameters or protects shared data, and calls only reentrant functions.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Semaphore Traces, Deadlock Handling and Driver Design

Textbooks keep semaphore values in two ways. In the RTOS convention the count never goes below zero: a take on a zero count puts the caller in a waiting queue, and a give with tasks waiting hands the unit straight to one of them without changing the count. In the Silberschatz blocking implementation, wait always decrements, so a value of -k means k tasks are waiting, and signal always increments and wakes one task if the result is still 0 or less. Both describe the same behaviour, so always state the convention when you write a trace.

Worked example 1: counting semaphore S = 2, four tasks, FIFO wake-up
Step       RTOS count  Silberschatz S  Waiting  Holding
A wait     1           1               -        A
B wait     0           0               -        A B
C wait     0           -1              C        A B
D wait     0           -2              C D      A B
A signal   0           -1              D        B C
B signal   0           0               -        C D
C signal   1           1               -        D
D signal   2           2               -        -

The order of the two waits in the producer matters. Waiting on empty before taking the lock means a producer that finds the buffer full sleeps without holding the lock, so the consumer can still get in and free a slot; reversing the order lets the producer sleep inside the critical section and deadlocks both tasks. The consumer mirrors the producer with wait(full), lock, remove at out, unlock and post(empty), and between operations empty + full = N.

concepts.plainText: count = (head - tail + N) mod N, head = next write slot, tail = next read slot; capacity N - 1 when one slot is kept empty

rows: Design so that one Coffman condition can never hold
Fixed global lock order, or request everything at once; may waste resources
Grant a request only if the system stays in a safe state
Banker's algorithm; needs every task's maximum claim in advance
Let deadlock happen, find a cycle in the wait-for graph, then abort or roll back a task
Periodic graph check; recovery loses work
Assume deadlock is rare and restart if it happens
Desktop OSes; a watchdog reset in embedded products

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: Banker's algorithm, one resource type, 10 units
Task  Allocated  Max  Need
A     3          7    4
B     2          4    2
C     2          6    4
Available = 10 - 7 = 3
B: need 2 <= 3 -> finishes, available 3 + 2 = 5
A: need 4 <= 5 -> finishes, available 8; C: need 4 <= 8 -> finishes
Safe sequence B, A, C, so the state is safe
Request: A asks for 2 more -> available 1; needs A 2, B 2, C 4
No task can finish with 1 unit -> unsafe, so A must wait
Rules for ISRs and deferred work:
items: Acknowledge or clear the interrupt source early; otherwise a level-triggered request fires again as soon as the ISR returns.
Do only the urgent part (read the data register, time-stamp, move bytes to a buffer) and defer the rest to a task or bottom half.
Use only non-blocking from-ISR kernel calls to give semaphores, post to queues or set event bits, and request a context switch on exit if a higher-priority task was woken.
Protect data shared with a task by briefly masking that interrupt inside the task, because the ISR cannot wait for a lock.
