Keep interrupt-disabled sections short: the longest one adds directly to the worst-case latency of every interrupt.

concepts.text: A typical interrupt-driven UART driver keeps a receive ring buffer and a transmit ring buffer. The receive ISR moves each byte from the data register into the RX buffer and gives a semaphore, so read() blocks only when the buffer is empty. write() copies bytes into the TX buffer and enables the transmit-empty interrupt, whose ISR sends one byte per interrupt and disables itself when the buffer runs dry. A polled driver instead checks the status register in a loop or periodic task; it is simpler and more deterministic, but an event can wait up to one full polling period before it is noticed.

Classic synchronisation bugs: taking the lock before the counting semaphore in a producer; giving a mutex from an ISR or from a task that does not own it; using a binary semaphore where several events can arrive before the task runs, so events are lost; leaving the transmit-empty interrupt enabled with nothing to send; and returning from an error path without releasing a lock.

For any semaphore trace, draw a table with one row per operation and columns for the value, the waiting queue and the holders, and say which convention you use. Check the answer with S = S0 - waits + signals: it always gives the final value in the negative-count convention, and in both conventions when no task is left waiting.

formulas.plainText: Semaphore value S = initial S0 - number of waits + number of signals (no task left blocked)
Fraction of CPU used by polling = time per poll x polls per second

notes.text: Mutex = ownership plus priority inheritance for locking; semaphore = signalling or counting, and it may be given from an ISR.
Forgetting volatile on a memory-mapped register or an ISR-shared flag lets the optimiser cache the value in a register, so a polling loop may never see the hardware change.
Deadlock is impossible if any one of the four Coffman conditions is broken; a fixed global lock order is the most common practical fix.

formulas.title: Semaphore count
formulas.plainText: S = S0 - waits + signals
formulas.description: Resulting counting-semaphore value after a sequence of wait and signal operations when no task remains blocked.

formulas.title: Polling overhead
formulas.plainText: Overhead = time per poll x polling frequency
formulas.description: Fraction of CPU time consumed by a polling driver, e.g. 10 µs x 1000 polls/s = 1%.

flashcards.back: An error where the result depends on the timing of concurrent accesses to shared data, e.g. a lost update from two unprotected count++ operations.

flashcards.front: Name the four necessary conditions for deadlock.
flashcards.back: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no pre-emption and circular wait (Coffman conditions).

flashcards.front: Why must ISRs be short and non-blocking?
flashcards.back: While an ISR runs, other interrupts and all tasks are delayed; blocking in an ISR would hang the system, so heavy work is deferred to a task.
It uses only local variables and parameters (or protects shared data) and calls only reentrant functions, so it can be interrupted and re-entered safely.

questions.questionText: A counting semaphore is initialised to 10. Tasks then perform 6 wait (P) operations and 4 signal (V) operations, and no task is left blocked. What is the final semaphore value?
questions.explanation: Each wait decrements and each signal increments: 10 - 6 + 4 = 8.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT one of the four necessary conditions for deadlock?
options: Hold and wait
Circular wait
Pre-emptive priority scheduling
Mutual exclusion
questions.explanation: The Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no pre-emption (of resources) and circular wait; pre-emptive CPU scheduling is not one of them.

questions.questionText: Why is the volatile qualifier used when declaring a pointer to a memory-mapped status register in embedded C?
options: To place the register in fast on-chip RAM
To make accesses to the register atomic
To stop the compiler optimising away or caching reads and writes of the register
To allow the register to be shared between processes
questions.explanation: volatile forces the compiler to perform every access because the value can change outside program control; it does not make accesses atomic.

questions.questionText: Which property distinguishes a mutex from a binary semaphore in most RTOSes?
options: A mutex has ownership and supports priority inheritance
A mutex can be given from an ISR
A mutex can count several identical resources
A mutex never causes a task to block
questions.explanation: Only the task that locked a mutex may unlock it, and RTOS mutexes usually implement priority inheritance; semaphores have no owner and may be given from ISRs.

questions.questionText: A correct solution to the critical-section problem must guarantee mutual exclusion, progress and which third property?
options: Pre-emption
Priority inheritance
Bounded waiting
Busy waiting
questions.explanation: Bounded waiting limits how many times other tasks may enter their critical sections after a task has asked to enter, so no task waits forever.

questions.questionText: On an 8-bit microcontroller, a timer ISR increments a 32-bit tick counter, and a task copies the counter with four separate byte reads. Occasionally the copied value is wrong by about 256. What is the simplest correct fix?
options: Declare the counter volatile and change nothing else
Disable (mask) the timer interrupt while the task copies the counter, then re-enable it
Protect the counter with a mutex taken by both the ISR and the task
Give the timer interrupt a higher priority
questions.explanation: The ISR can run between the byte reads, so the task combines bytes from before and after a carry. volatile only forces the reads to happen and an ISR must never take a mutex, whereas a short interrupt-masked copy makes the read atomic.

questions.questionText: Two tasks each execute count = count + 1 five times on a shared variable count that starts at 0. Each increment is a separate load, add and store, and the scheduler may switch tasks between any two of these steps. What are the smallest and largest possible final values of count?
options: 2 and 10
5 and 10
0 and 10
1 and 10
questions.explanation: 10 needs no overlap at all. For the minimum, T1 loads 0 and stalls while T2 does four increments, T1 stores 1, then T2 loads 1 and stalls while T1 finishes its last four, and T2 finally stores 2; an exhaustive search of all interleavings confirms that 2 is the least possible value.

questions.questionText: Shared variable x starts at 1. Task T1 executes x = x + 1 and task T2 executes x = 2 * x, each compiled as one load followed by one store, with no locking. Which final values of x are possible?
options: 3 or 4 only
4 only
2 or 4 only
questions.explanation: The serial orders give (1 + 1) x 2 = 4 and 2 x 1 + 1 = 3. If both tasks load 1 before either stores, the last store wins and leaves 2 (from 1 + 1 or from 2 x 1).

questions.questionText: On a single-core microcontroller, which of these does NOT by itself protect a critical section shared by two tasks?
options: Disabling interrupts around the access
Declaring the shared variable volatile
Taking a mutex around the access in both tasks
Locking the scheduler around the access when no ISR uses the data
questions.explanation: volatile only stops the compiler from caching or removing accesses; it does not make a read-modify-write sequence indivisible. The other three methods stop the other task from running in the middle of the sequence.

questions.questionText: Four identical DMA channels are shared by several tasks, and a counting semaphore controls access to them. What should its initial value be?
questions.explanation: A counting semaphore that manages identical resources starts at the number of units; each take reserves one channel and each give returns it.

questions.questionText: A counting semaphore starts at 2. In this RTOS the count never goes below 0: a take when the count is 0 blocks the caller, and a give with tasks waiting hands the unit straight to the longest-waiting task. The operations are: T1 take, T2 take, T3 take, T1 give, T4 take, T2 give. What is the final state?
options: Count 0; T2 and T3 hold units and T4 is still waiting
Count 1; T3 holds a unit because T4's take failed
Count 2; the two gives restored both units
Count 0; T3 and T4 hold units and no task is waiting
questions.explanation: T1 and T2 take both units (count 0) and T3 blocks. T1's give hands its unit to T3, T4 then blocks, and T2's give hands its unit to T4, so the count stays 0 with T3 and T4 holding units.

questions.questionText: Semaphore S = 1 uses the blocking implementation in which wait decrements S and blocks the caller if S becomes negative, and signal increments S and wakes the first waiting process if S is then 0 or less. The sequence is: P1 wait, P2 wait, P3 wait, P1 signal, P2 signal. What is S at the end, and which process is in the critical section?
options: S = 0, and P3 is in the critical section
S = 1, and no process is in the critical section
S = -1, and P3 is still blocked
S = 0, and P2 is in the critical section
questions.explanation: S goes 1 → 0 (P1 enters) → -1 → -2 (P2 and P3 blocked). P1's signal makes S = -1 and wakes P2; P2's signal makes S = 0 and wakes P3, which now holds the critical section with nobody waiting.

questions.questionText: An ISR gives a semaphore three times while the handling task is busy with other work and is not waiting on it. The task then takes the semaphore repeatedly until a take would block. How many takes succeed with a binary semaphore (initially 0), and with a counting semaphore (initial count 0, maximum 10)?
options: 3 with both
1 with both
0 with the binary semaphore and 3 with the counting semaphore
1 with the binary semaphore and 3 with the counting semaphore
questions.explanation: A binary semaphore saturates at 1, so the second and third gives are lost and only one take succeeds, while a counting semaphore reaches 3 and records all three events. Use a counting semaphore or a queue when events can arrive faster than the task handles them.

questions.questionText: Statement A in task T1 must always execute before statement B in task T2. Using one semaphore S, which arrangement guarantees this for every interleaving?
options: S starts at 1; T1 does A then signal(S); T2 does wait(S) then B
S starts at 0; T1 does A then signal(S); T2 does wait(S) then B
S starts at 0; T1 does A then wait(S); T2 does signal(S) then B
S starts at 0; T1 does wait(S) then A; T2 does B then signal(S)
questions.explanation: With S = 0, T2's wait cannot succeed until T1 has executed A and signalled. Starting at 1 lets T2 pass at once, the third arrangement does not constrain B at all, and the fourth forces B before A.

questions.questionText: Tasks A and B must each reach a meeting point before either continues past it. At the meeting point A executes signal(SA); wait(SB) and B executes signal(SB); wait(SA). What initial values must SA and SB have?
options: SA = 1 and SB = 1
SA = 0 and SB = 0
SA = 1 and SB = 0
SA = 0 and SB = 1
questions.explanation: Each task may pass its wait only after the other has signalled on arrival, so both semaphores must start at 0; any initial 1 lets one task pass before the other arrives. Signalling before waiting also avoids the deadlock that wait-then-signal would cause.

questions.questionText:
Semaphores S1 and S2 both start at 0, and three tasks run concurrently in any interleaving:

T1: print A; signal(S1); wait(S2); print E
T2: wait(S1); print B; signal(S2); print C
T3: print D

Which output can NOT occur?
options: DABCE
ADBEC
ABCED
AEBCD
questions.explanation: B can be printed only after T1's signal(S1), so A comes before B, and E can be printed only after T2's signal(S2), which follows B, so E comes after B. AEBCD breaks the second rule, while D and the relative order of C and E are unconstrained.

questions.questionText: Task T locks a recursive mutex three times through nested function calls and then unlocks it twice. Task U now tries to lock the same mutex. What happens?
options: U blocks, because T still owns the mutex with a lock count of 1
U gets the mutex, because T has already unlocked it
T deadlocked itself on its second lock
The RTOS returns an error because a mutex cannot be locked twice
questions.explanation: A recursive mutex counts nested locks by its owner and is released only after the owner has unlocked it as many times as it locked it. With a non-recursive mutex, T would have deadlocked on its second lock.

questions.questionText: Why must an interrupt service routine never try to take a mutex?
options: Only the idle task is allowed to take a mutex
Taking a mutex resets the interrupt controller
A mutex can be shared by at most two tasks
An ISR cannot block, and mutex ownership and priority inheritance apply only to tasks
questions.explanation: If the mutex were already held, the ISR would have to wait, but it has no task context to block in, so the system would hang. ISRs signal tasks with semaphores, queues or event bits instead.

questions.questionText: A system requires every task to request all the resources it will ever need in one call before it starts running. Which deadlock condition does this rule break?
options: Hold and wait
Circular wait
Mutual exclusion
No pre-emption
questions.explanation: A task never holds some resources while waiting for others, so hold and wait cannot occur; the price is poor resource utilisation and possible starvation.

questions.questionText: Which statement about resource-allocation graphs is correct?
options: A cycle always means deadlock, whatever the number of instances
Deadlock can exist even when the graph has no cycle
With single-instance resources, a cycle never means deadlock
If every resource has a single instance, a cycle means deadlock; with several instances per resource, a cycle is necessary but not sufficient
questions.explanation: With several instances, a task in the cycle may still receive a unit released by a task outside the cycle, so the cycle can break by itself; with single instances nobody else can release the resources in the cycle.

questions.questionText: In a wait-for graph, T1 waits for T2, T2 waits for T3, T3 waits for T1 and T4 waits for T2; each wait is for one resource held by the other task. What is the fewest tasks that must be aborted so that all remaining tasks can finish?
options: Only T4
All four tasks
Two tasks: T2 and T4
One task from the cycle T1 → T2 → T3
questions.explanation: The cycle T1-T2-T3 is the deadlock; aborting any one of them releases its resource, the rest of the cycle finishes in turn, and T4 then gets what it is waiting for. Aborting T4 alone breaks nothing.

questions.questionText: A system has 12 units of one resource type. Current allocations and maximum claims are: P0 holds 4 (max 9), P1 holds 2 (max 5), P2 holds 3 (max 7) and P3 holds 1 (max 3). Using the Banker's algorithm, which single request can be granted immediately while keeping the system safe?
options: P0 requests 1 unit
P3 requests 1 unit
P1 requests 1 unit
P2 requests 1 unit
questions.explanation: Available = 12 - 10 = 2 and the needs are 5, 3, 4 and 2. Granting P3 one unit leaves 1 available with P3 needing only 1, so P3 can finish (available 3), then P1, P2 and P0; any other grant leaves 1 unit while every need is at least 2, so no task could finish.

questions.questionText: What distinguishes starvation from deadlock?
options: Starvation needs a cycle of waiting tasks, and deadlock does not
Deadlock always clears itself after a timeout, and starvation never does
In starvation one task waits indefinitely while others keep running; in deadlock a set of tasks all wait for each other and none can proceed
They are two names for the same situation
questions.explanation: A starving task could run if it were ever chosen, for example a low-priority task that is always passed over, whereas deadlocked tasks are stuck by their mutual waits whatever the scheduler does.

questions.questionText: The Banker's algorithm, which grants a request only if the system stays in a safe state, is an example of which deadlock-handling strategy?
options: Deadlock prevention
Deadlock avoidance
Deadlock detection and recovery
Ignoring deadlock (the ostrich approach)
questions.explanation: Avoidance decides at run time, from each task's declared maximum claim, whether granting a request could lead to deadlock; prevention instead removes one of the four conditions by design.

questions.questionText: A bounded-buffer producer is written as wait(mutex); wait(empty); insert item; signal(mutex); signal(full), while the consumer uses wait(full); wait(mutex); remove item; signal(mutex); signal(empty). What can happen when the buffer is full?
options: The producer overwrites the oldest item in the buffer
Nothing goes wrong, because the order of the two waits never matters
The producer blocks on empty while holding mutex, the consumer then blocks on mutex, and both are deadlocked
The consumer removes an item without locking and corrupts the buffer
questions.explanation: With the buffer full, empty = 0, so the producer sleeps inside the critical section and the consumer can never get mutex to free a slot. Taking the counting semaphore before the mutex, as in the standard solution, avoids this.

questions.questionText: Which RTOS object holds at most one message (often a pointer), so that a further post blocks or overwrites until the receiver has taken it?
options: Pipe
Mailbox
Counting semaphore
Event group
questions.explanation: A mailbox is a single-slot message holder; a message queue holds several messages and a pipe carries a byte stream.

questions.questionText: Which inter-task mechanism carries an unstructured stream of bytes from a writer task to a reader task, in FIFO order and without message boundaries?
options: Mailbox
Mutex
Pipe
Event flags
questions.explanation: A pipe is a byte-stream FIFO: the reader may take any number of bytes regardless of how they were written, unlike a queue of fixed-size messages.

questions.questionText: A message queue has room for 3 messages. Before the receiver runs, the sender posts m1, m2, m3, m4 and m5 with a non-blocking send that fails (returns an error) when the queue is full. The receiver then reads twice. Which messages does it read, and what is left in the queue?
options: It reads m1 and m2; m3 is left, and m4 and m5 were never queued
It reads m4 and m5; m3 is left
It reads m1 and m2; m3, m4 and m5 are left
It reads m3 and m4; m5 is left
questions.explanation: Only m1 to m3 fit, and the sends of m4 and m5 fail because the queue is full. A FIFO queue delivers the oldest messages first, so the two reads return m1 and m2 and leave m3.

questions.questionText: During a 100 ms burst an ISR posts 500 messages per second to a queue, while the consumer task removes 300 messages per second. Treating both as steady rates, what is the smallest queue length that avoids losing messages during the burst?
options: 20 messages
50 messages
30 messages
80 messages
questions.explanation: The queue grows at 500 - 300 = 200 messages/s, so after 0.1 s it holds 200 x 0.1 = 20 messages; 50 would ignore the consumer.

questions.questionText: A task sends 2 KB frames through an RTOS queue that copies every message by value. What is the usual way to avoid copying 2 KB on each send and receive?
options: Make the queue longer
Send the frame through a binary semaphore instead
Send a pointer to a buffer taken from a memory pool, and let the receiver return the buffer to the pool when it has finished
Declare the frame volatile
questions.explanation: Only the small pointer is copied and ownership of the buffer passes with the message, so the sender must not touch the buffer until the receiver releases it.

questions.questionText: A task waits on an event group for bits 0 and 2 with the 'wait for all bits' option and 'clear bits on exit'. The group currently holds 0x0C (binary 1100). An ISR now sets bit 0. What happens?
options: The task stays blocked because bit 1 is not set
The task wakes, and the group is left holding 0x0D
The task wakes, and the group is left holding 0x08
The task had already woken while the group held 0x0C
questions.explanation: After the ISR the group holds 0x0D, which has both bit 0 and bit 2 set, so the wait-for-all condition is met; clearing bits 0 and 2 on exit leaves 0x0D AND NOT 0x05 = 0x08. With 'wait for any bit' the task would already have woken at 0x0C.

questions.questionText: In an RTOS or POSIX system, what is a signal?
options: A hardware request line from a peripheral to the interrupt controller
A counting semaphore that only ISRs may use
A message queue with exactly one slot
An asynchronous software notification sent to a task that makes it run a registered handler, much like a software interrupt
questions.explanation: A signal interrupts the normal flow of the receiving task or process and runs its handler; it carries little or no data, unlike a queue or mailbox.

questions.questionText: A task must wait until BOTH an 'ADC conversion done' event and a 'DMA transfer done' event have occurred, in either order. Which single kernel object suits this best?
options: A mutex
A binary semaphore
An event group (event flags) with a wait-for-all-bits call
A pipe
questions.explanation: Each event sets its own bit and the task sleeps until both bits are set; a single binary semaphore cannot tell which event occurred.

questions.questionText: Which of these is safe to do inside an ISR in a typical RTOS?
options: Wait on a message queue with a 10 ms timeout
Give a semaphore with the from-ISR version of the call
Take a mutex that protects a shared buffer
Call a delay function to wait for the device to settle
questions.explanation: ISRs must never block. The from-ISR calls only give or post without waiting, and they report whether a higher-priority task was woken so the kernel can switch tasks on exit.

questions.questionText: For a UART receive interrupt, which division of work between the ISR and a task is best?
options: ISR: parse each complete frame and update the display; no task is needed
ISR: only signal the task; task: read the data register later
ISR: disable all interrupts until the task has finished with the byte
ISR: copy the byte from the data register into a ring buffer and signal the task; task: parse and act on the received messages
questions.explanation: Reading the data register at once prevents an overrun, and the slow parsing runs later at task level, keeping the ISR short. Leaving the byte in the register risks it being overwritten by the next one.

questions.questionText: Which statement about splitting interrupt handling into a top half and a bottom half is correct?
options: The top half does the minimum urgent work in interrupt context; the bottom half runs later, with interrupts enabled, and can take longer
The bottom half runs first and the top half is deferred to a task
The bottom half must run with all interrupts disabled
The split lengthens the time for which interrupts are disabled
questions.explanation: In Linux the bottom half is a softirq, tasklet or workqueue item; in an RTOS it is usually a task woken by the ISR. Deferring work shortens interrupt-disabled time and so lowers the latency of other interrupts.

questions.questionText: Interrupt X has the lowest priority of three interrupt sources. The longest code section that runs with interrupts disabled lasts 20 µs, the two higher-priority ISRs take 15 µs and 10 µs and each can occur at most once in the interval, and X's own ISR takes 8 µs. Ignoring entry and exit overheads, what is the worst-case time from X's request to the end of its ISR?
options: 28 µs
45 µs
53 µs
33 µs
questions.explanation: In the worst case X is raised just as interrupts are disabled for 20 µs, both higher-priority interrupts are pending when they are re-enabled and run first (15 + 10 µs), and then X runs for 8 µs: 20 + 15 + 10 + 8 = 53 µs.

questions.questionText: An interrupt-driven UART transmit driver enables the 'transmit register empty' interrupt whenever write() puts bytes into its software buffer. What must the ISR do when it finds the software buffer empty?
options: Disable the transmit-empty interrupt, because otherwise it fires again immediately and keeps firing
Send a 0x00 byte to keep the line busy
Block on a semaphore until more data is written
Re-enable global interrupts and return without changing anything
questions.explanation: The empty condition stays true while there is nothing to send, so the interrupt would repeat endlessly and starve the CPU; write() re-enables it when new data arrives.

questions.questionText: Which device-driver entry point is normally used for device-specific control operations, such as setting a UART's baud rate?
options: read
open
ioctl
close
questions.explanation: ioctl (I/O control) carries device-specific commands and parameters that do not fit the generic read and write calls.

questions.questionText: In which situation is a polled driver usually a better choice than an interrupt-driven one?
options: The device is almost always ready, or must be checked at a fixed rate anyway, and the code is a simple loop
The event is rare and occurs at unpredictable times
The CPU should sleep in a low-power mode until the event happens
The system must react as fast as possible to a rare event
questions.explanation: Polling costs little when the device is nearly always ready and gives simple, deterministic timing; rare or unpredictable events, fast reaction and low-power sleep all favour interrupts.

questions.questionText: A driver checks a device status flag from a periodic task every 5 ms. The event can occur at any instant. Ignoring task scheduling delays, what are the worst-case and average delays from the event to the poll that detects it?
options: 2.5 ms worst case and 1.25 ms on average
5 ms worst case and 5 ms on average
5 ms worst case and 2.5 ms on average
10 ms worst case and 5 ms on average
questions.explanation: An event just after a poll waits a full period of 5 ms, and with events spread evenly over the period the mean wait is half of it, 2.5 ms. An interrupt-driven driver would respond within the interrupt latency instead.

questions.questionText: Which order, from the application down to the hardware, matches a typical layered embedded I/O stack?
options: Application → low-level driver (HAL) → RTOS/OS I/O API → device-independent driver layer → device registers
Application → RTOS/OS I/O API → device-independent driver layer → low-level driver (HAL) → device registers
Application → device-independent driver layer → device registers → low-level driver (HAL) → RTOS/OS I/O API
Application → RTOS/OS I/O API → low-level driver (HAL) → device-independent driver layer → device registers
questions.explanation: Each layer hides the one below it: the application uses generic calls such as read and write, the device-independent layer handles buffering and naming, and only the low-level driver or HAL touches the memory-mapped or port registers.

questions.questionText: A 64-slot ring buffer tells full from empty by always leaving one slot unused (it is full when (head + 1) mod 64 = tail). At most how many items can it hold?
questions.explanation: One slot is sacrificed so that head = tail can mean empty without ambiguity, leaving 64 - 1 = 63 usable slots.

Because one slot is always left empty, the first loop stores 7 bytes (head = 7). After tail = 3 only 3 more fit (head goes 7 → 0 → 1 → 2, then next = 3 = tail), so ok = 10 and (2 - 3 + 8) % 8 = 7 bytes are waiting.

questions.questionText: A bounded buffer with 4 slots uses semaphores empty (initially 4) and full (initially 0) plus a mutex; semaphore counts never go below 0, and a signal with a task waiting hands the unit straight to that task. The producer has higher priority than the consumer and tries to insert 6 items back to back. The consumer then removes exactly one item and goes to sleep on a timer. Once the producer can make no more progress, what are empty and full, and how many items has it inserted?
options: empty = 1 and full = 3; 4 items inserted
empty = 0 and full = 4; 6 items inserted
empty = 0 and full = 3; 5 items inserted
empty = 0 and full = 4; 5 items inserted, with the producer blocked on its 6th
questions.explanation: The producer inserts 4 items (empty 0, full 4) and blocks on wait(empty). The consumer's wait(full) makes full 3, and its signal(empty) wakes the producer, which inserts item 5 (full 4) and blocks again on item 6 with empty still 0.

questions.questionText: A bounded buffer of N slots is protected by the semaphores empty and full and a binary semaphore mutex. What are their initial values?
options: empty = 0, full = N, mutex = 1
empty = N, full = N, mutex = 0
empty = 1, full = 0, mutex = N
empty = N, full = 0, mutex = 1
questions.explanation: Initially every slot is free (empty = N), no item is available (full = 0) and the buffer is unlocked (mutex = 1).

questions.questionText: On a single-core microcontroller with a pre-emptive priority RTOS, a high-priority task busy-waits in a loop on a flag that only a lower-priority task sets. What happens?
options: Both tasks are stuck for good: the spinning task never lets the lower-priority task run, so the flag is never set
The spinning task wastes some CPU time but soon proceeds
The kernel raises the lower-priority task's priority until it sets the flag
The tick interrupt time-slices the two tasks, so the flag is set within one tick
questions.explanation: Priority scheduling never runs a lower-priority task while a higher-priority one is ready, and a spinning task is always ready. It should block on a semaphore or event instead; priority inheritance applies to mutexes, not to busy-wait flags.

questions.questionText: Peterson's solution for processes P0 and P1 uses flag[2] and turn. To enter, Pi sets flag[i] = true, then turn = j (the other process), and waits while flag[j] && turn == j. Both try to enter at once: P0 sets flag[0], P1 sets flag[1], P0 sets turn = 1, and then P1 sets turn = 0. Which process enters its critical section first?
options: P1, because it was the last to write turn
P0, because the last write left turn = 0, so only P1 has to wait
Both, because both flags are true
Neither, because both processes wait forever
questions.explanation: P0 waits only while flag[1] && turn == 1, which is false once turn = 0, while P1 waits while flag[0] && turn == 0, which is true. The process that writes turn last defers to the other, which gives mutual exclusion and progress.

questions.questionText: Four tasks share identical units of one resource type. Each task needs at most 3 units, acquires them one at a time and releases them only when it finishes. What is the smallest number of units that makes deadlock impossible?
questions.explanation: Deadlock needs every task stuck holding fewer than 3 units: with 4 x 2 = 8 units all four can each hold 2 and wait forever. One more unit, 4(3 - 1) + 1 = 9, guarantees that some task can always complete and release its units.

questions.questionText: A counting semaphore guards 3 identical buffers and wakes waiting tasks in FIFO order. Tasks request a buffer at these times and keep it for these durations: T1 at 0 ms for 6 ms, T2 at 1 ms for 3 ms, T3 at 2 ms for 5 ms, T4 at 3 ms for 2 ms and T5 at 5 ms for 3 ms. Ignoring CPU time, when does T5 obtain a buffer, and when is the last buffer released?
options: T5 gets a buffer at 5 ms, and the last buffer is released at 8 ms
T5 gets a buffer at 7 ms, and the last buffer is released at 10 ms
T5 gets a buffer at 4 ms, and the last buffer is released at 7 ms
T5 gets a buffer at 6 ms, and the last buffer is released at 9 ms
questions.explanation: T1 to T3 take the three buffers; T4 waits until T2 releases at 4 ms and keeps a buffer until 6 ms. At 5 ms none is free (T1 until 6, T3 until 7, T4 until 6), so T5 gets one at 6 ms and releases it at 9 ms, the last release.

subtopics.title: Open-Loop & Closed-Loop Control Systems
subtopics.subtitle: Feedback, closed-loop gain, performance measures, on-off and PID control, digital loops

concepts.text: Control System Vocabulary
Basic terms used in every control loop:
items: Plant (process): the physical system being controlled, e.g. a room, motor or tank.
Controller: computes the control action from the error or the reference input.
Actuator: converts the controller output into physical action (heater, motor driver, valve).
Sensor (transducer): measures the output, e.g. thermistor, encoder, pressure sensor.
Setpoint (reference r): the desired value of the output.
Error e = r - y: difference between setpoint and measured output y.
Disturbance: an unwanted external input that changes the output (open window, load torque).

concepts.text: Open-Loop vs Closed-Loop

rows: None; output does not affect the control action
Output measured and compared with setpoint
Can oscillate or become unstable if badly tuned
Timer toaster, washing machine timer, traffic light on fixed timing
Thermostat, cruise control, servo motor, PID loops

concepts.text: Open-loop block diagram in words: reference input goes into the controller, then the actuator, then the plant, giving the output; nothing flows back. Closed-loop block diagram: the reference enters a summing junction, which subtracts the fed-back sensor signal to form the error; the error drives the controller G_c and plant G_p to give the output, and the sensor H feeds the output back to the summing junction. With negative feedback the loop continually acts to drive the error toward zero.

concepts.plainText: Closed-loop gain T = G / (1 + GH) for negative feedback

concepts.text: Performance Measures
Step-response and loop quality measures:
items: Stability: a bounded input gives a bounded output; the response settles instead of growing or oscillating forever.
Steady-state error: the error left after transients die out; for a unity-feedback type-0 system with a step input e_ss = 1/(1 + K_p).
Overshoot: how far the output goes beyond the setpoint, usually as a percentage.
Rise time: time to go from 10% to 90% of the final value.
Settling time: time to stay within a band (2% or 5%) of the final value.
Negative feedback reduces sensitivity to plant changes by the factor 1 + GH, at the cost of lower gain.

concepts.text: On-off (bang-bang) control is the simplest closed-loop controller: the actuator is fully on when the error is positive and fully off when it is negative. A household thermostat or refrigerator uses it with hysteresis (a dead band such as +/-0.5 °C) so the relay does not chatter around the setpoint. The output therefore oscillates in a small band rather than settling exactly.
P, PI and PID Control

concepts.latex: u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int_0^t e(\tau)\,d\tau + K_d \frac{de(t)}{dt}
concepts.plainText: u(t) = Kp*e(t) + Ki*integral of e dt + Kd*de/dt

rows: Zero steady-state error with fair speed

concepts.text: Digital Control Loop
A microcontroller implements the loop once every sampling period T:
items: Sample the sensor through an ADC at a fixed rate driven by a timer interrupt or periodic RTOS task.
Compute error and the discrete control law, e.g. u[k] = Kp e[k] + Ki T sum(e) + Kd (e[k] - e[k-1])/T.
Output through a DAC or PWM to the actuator driver.
Choose T well below the plant's time constants (often 10 to 20 times faster); jitter in T degrades control, which is why control tasks get high RMS priority.
Clamp the output and stop integrating when saturated to avoid integral windup.

concepts.text: Worked thermostat example: setpoint 22 °C, measured temperature 19 °C, so e = 22 - 19 = 3 °C. With a proportional controller Kp = 10 % per °C the heater is driven at u = 10 x 3 = 30% power. As the room warms to 21 °C the error falls to 1 °C and power to 10%; a pure P controller leaves a small steady-state error because some error is needed to keep the heater on, and adding an integral term removes it.
Going Deeper: Feedback Analysis and Digital PID

The closed-loop gain follows from two equations read off the block diagram. The summing junction gives E = R − HC and the forward path gives C = G·E, so C = G(R − HC), which rearranges to C(1 + GH) = G·R and C/R = G/(1 + GH). With positive feedback the junction adds the fed-back signal, giving G/(1 − GH), which grows without limit as GH approaches 1. The product GH is the loop gain, and a disturbance D entering at the plant output is reduced by the same factor, appearing at the output as D/(1 + GH).

concepts.plainText: Sensitivity of the closed-loop gain T to the forward gain G: S = (dT/T)/(dG/G) = 1/(1 + GH)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: G = 200, H = 0.05  ->  loop gain GH = 10
T = 200 / (1 + 10)                          = 18.18
G falls 20 % to 160:  GH = 8,  T = 160 / 9  = 17.78
Change in T = (17.78 - 18.18) / 18.18       = -2.2 %  (open loop: -20 %)
Small-change estimate: S = 1/(1 + GH) = 0.091, 0.091 x 20 % = 1.8 %
Output disturbance of 30 rpm -> 30 / (1 + 10) = 2.7 rpm remains

With a proportional gain Kp driving a plant of DC gain Kplant in a unity-feedback loop, the loop gain is K = Kp·Kplant, the output settles at K/(1 + K) of the setpoint and the steady-state error is 1/(1 + K) of the step. The error cannot reach zero because the plant needs a non-zero drive and a P controller produces drive only from error; raising Kp shrinks the offset but increases overshoot and eventually threatens stability. Closing the loop around a first-order plant K/(τs + 1) also speeds it up: the closed-loop transfer function K/(τs + 1 + K) has time constant τ/(1 + K), and the 2% settling time is about four time constants. For example, τ = 15 s and K = 4 give a closed-loop time constant of 3 s, a settling time near 12 s and a final value of 0.8 of the setpoint.

rows: Overshoot rises; settling time changes little

concepts.text: Practical details used when tuning and implementing controllers:
items: Ziegler–Nichols ultimate-gain method: with I and D off, raise Kp until the loop oscillates steadily at gain Ku with period Pu, then set Kp = 0.6 Ku, Ti = Pu/2 and Td = Pu/8 for PID (P only: Kp = 0.5 Ku; PI: Kp = 0.45 Ku, Ti = Pu/1.2).
The standard and parallel PID forms are linked by Ki = Kp/Ti and Kd = Kp·Td, so a longer integral time Ti means weaker integral action.

On-off control with switching points L and H: heating time = (H − L)/heating rate and cooling time = (H − L)/cooling rate; a narrower band gives a smaller swing but more frequent switching and relay wear.
Integral windup: while the actuator is saturated the integral keeps growing and later causes a large overshoot, so the integral is clamped or integration is stopped during saturation.
Derivative kick: a setpoint step makes de/dt very large for one sample, so many controllers differentiate the measurement instead of the error and low-pass filter the D term to limit noise.

concepts.latex: \Delta u_k = K_p(e_k - e_{k-1}) + K_i T e_k + \frac{K_d}{T}(e_k - 2e_{k-1} + e_{k-2})
concepts.plainText: Velocity (incremental) PID: Δu[k] = Kp(e[k] − e[k−1]) + Ki·T·e[k] + (Kd/T)(e[k] − 2e[k−1] + e[k−2]), then u[k] = u[k−1] + Δu[k]

concepts.text: A continuous closed-loop system is stable when every root of its characteristic equation 1 + G(s)H(s) = 0, i.e. every closed-loop pole, has a negative real part and so lies in the left half of the s-plane. For G = K/(s(s + 6)) with unity feedback the equation is s² + 6s + K = 0: K = 5 gives real poles at −1 and −5, while K above 9 gives a complex pair with an oscillatory, overshooting response. A sampled loop is stable when its poles lie inside the unit circle; the plant y[k+1] = a·y[k] + b·u[k] under u[k] = Kp(r − y[k]) has the single pole a − b·Kp, so it is stable only while |a − b·Kp| < 1. Extra loop delay, such as a long sampling period or slow computation, adds phase lag and lowers the gain at which oscillation starts.

Common mistakes: using G/(1 + GH) for a positive-feedback loop; writing the step error of a P loop as 1/K instead of 1/(1 + K); forgetting the sampling period in the discrete integral (Ki·T·Σe) and derivative ((e[k] − e[k−1])/T) terms; quoting the integral time Ti or derivative time Td as if they were the gains Ki and Kd; and letting the integrator wind up while the actuator is saturated.

formulas.plainText: Closed-loop gain T = G / (1 + GH)

formulas.latex: u(t) = K_p e + K_i \int e\,dt + K_d \frac{de}{dt}
formulas.plainText: PID law u = Kp*e + Ki*integral(e dt) + Kd*de/dt
Steady-state error to a unit step, type-0 unity feedback: e_ss = 1/(1 + K_pos)

formulas.latex: u[k] = K_p e[k] + K_i T \sum_{j=0}^{k} e[j] + K_d \frac{e[k] - e[k-1]}{T}
formulas.plainText: Discrete PID: u[k] = Kp e[k] + Ki T sum e[j] + Kd (e[k] - e[k-1])/T

notes.text: Link each PID term to its job: P for speed, I for zero steady-state error, D for damping and reduced overshoot.
If GH is much greater than 1, T = G/(1 + GH) is approximately 1/H: the closed-loop gain depends mainly on the feedback sensor, not on the plant.
Feedback can destabilise a system: too much gain or too much loop delay causes oscillation, which is why closed-loop systems must be tuned and checked for stability.

formulas.title: Closed-loop gain
formulas.plainText: T = G / (1 + GH)
formulas.description: Overall gain of a negative-feedback loop with forward gain G and feedback gain H.

formulas.title: PID control law
formulas.latex: u(t) = K_p e + K_i \int e\,dt + K_d \frac{de}{dt}
formulas.plainText: u = Kp e + Ki integral(e) dt + Kd de/dt
formulas.description: Controller output as the sum of proportional, integral and derivative actions on the error.

formulas.title: Step steady-state error
formulas.plainText: e_ss = 1/(1 + K_pos)
formulas.description: Residual error of a unity-feedback type-0 system to a unit step, where K_pos is the loop DC gain.

formulas.title: Discrete PID
formulas.latex: u[k] = K_p e[k] + K_i T \sum e[j] + K_d \frac{e[k] - e[k-1]}{T}
formulas.plainText: u[k] = Kp e[k] + Ki T sum e + Kd (e[k]-e[k-1])/T
formulas.description: Sampled form of PID executed once per sampling period T in a microcontroller.

flashcards.front: Give one example each of open-loop and closed-loop control.
flashcards.back: Open-loop: timer-based toaster or washing machine; closed-loop: thermostat-controlled heater or car cruise control.

flashcards.front: Which PID term removes steady-state error?
flashcards.back: The integral term, because it keeps accumulating any remaining error until the error is zero.

flashcards.front: What is the closed-loop gain of a negative-feedback system?
flashcards.back: T = G/(1 + GH), where G is the forward-path gain and H the feedback gain.

flashcards.front: Why does an on-off thermostat use hysteresis?
flashcards.back: A dead band around the setpoint stops the relay switching rapidly (chattering) when the temperature hovers near the setpoint.

questions.questionText: A negative-feedback system has forward gain G = 100 and feedback gain H = 0.09. What is the closed-loop gain?
In a PID controller, which term is mainly responsible for eliminating steady-state error?
options: Derivative term
Proportional term
Integral term
Feedforward term
questions.explanation: The integral term accumulates past error and keeps changing the output until the error is zero; P alone leaves a residual error and D only reacts to changes.

questions.questionText: A unity-feedback type-0 system has a DC loop gain of 9. What is its steady-state error for a unit step input?
Which of the following is an open-loop control system?
options: A room air conditioner controlled by a thermostat
A toaster that heats bread for a time set on a dial
A car cruise control holding a set speed
A water-tank float valve that closes as the level rises
questions.explanation: The toaster's heating time never depends on how brown the bread actually is, so no output information is fed back. The thermostat, cruise control and float valve all measure the output (temperature, speed, level) and correct the action.

questions.questionText: A feedback loop is rewired so that the fed-back signal is added to the reference (positive feedback). With forward gain G = 5 and feedback gain H = 0.1, what is the closed-loop gain?
questions.explanation: Positive feedback gives T = G/(1 − GH) = 5/(1 − 0.5) = 10. 3.33 is the negative-feedback value 5/(1 + 0.5) and 0.5 is the loop gain GH.

questions.questionText: Two blocks with gains G1 = 5 and G2 = 6 are connected in cascade in the forward path of a negative-feedback loop whose feedback gain is H = 0.1. What is the overall closed-loop gain?
questions.explanation: Cascaded blocks multiply: G = 5 × 6 = 30, so T = 30/(1 + 30 × 0.1) = 30/4 = 7.5. Adding the gains gives 11/2.1 = 5.24, 30 is the open-loop gain and 10 is 1/H.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a closed-loop control system?
options: Traffic lights switching on a fixed timing plan
A washing machine running a fixed timed programme
An automatic voltage regulator that measures the generator output voltage and adjusts the field current
An electric fan with a three-position speed switch
questions.explanation: The voltage regulator compares the measured output voltage with the reference and corrects the error, which is feedback. The other three run preset actions without measuring the result.

questions.questionText: An amplifier with forward gain G = 200 must give a closed-loop gain of exactly 10 using negative feedback. What feedback gain H is needed?
questions.explanation: 10 = 200/(1 + 200H) gives 1 + 200H = 20, so H = 19/200 = 0.095. H = 0.1 is the 1/T approximation, which would actually give 200/21 = 9.52.

questions.questionText: A negative-feedback system has loop gain GH = 49. If the forward gain G increases by 10% while H is unchanged, by approximately what percentage does the closed-loop gain change?
questions.explanation: Sensitivity S = 1/(1 + GH) = 1/50 = 0.02, so ΔT/T ≈ 0.02 × 10% = 0.2% (recomputing exactly gives 0.18%). Without feedback the gain would change by the full 10%.

questions.questionText: In a closed-loop control system, which element measures the controlled output and converts it into a signal that can be compared with the setpoint?
options: Actuator
Plant
Controller
Sensor (transducer)
questions.explanation: The sensor, e.g. a thermistor or encoder, provides the feedback signal. The actuator applies power to the plant and the controller computes the action from the error.

questions.questionText: An open-loop motor drive slows by 50 rpm when a load torque is applied. The drive is then placed in a negative-feedback speed loop with loop gain GH = 24, the load acting as a disturbance at the output. By how much does the speed now drop?
options: 50 rpm
25 rpm
2 rpm
48 rpm
questions.explanation: An output disturbance is divided by 1 + GH, so the drop becomes 50/(1 + 24) = 2 rpm. 48 rpm is the part of the drop that feedback removes, not the part that remains.

questions.questionText: Compared with an open-loop system, what is the main drawback of a closed-loop control system?
options: It cannot correct for disturbances acting on the plant
Its accuracy depends entirely on the calibration of the plant
It can oscillate or become unstable if the loop gain or loop delay is too large
It needs no sensor, so faults go undetected
questions.explanation: Feedback adds a sensor, cost and the risk of instability when the gain or delay is too high. Disturbance rejection and insensitivity to plant calibration are advantages of closed loop, and needing no sensor describes open loop.

questions.questionText: A microcontroller keeps a room warm: a thermistor measures the temperature and a solid-state relay switches the heater element on and off. In control-system terms, the relay together with the heater element is the:
options: Sensor
Controller
Disturbance
Actuator
questions.explanation: The actuator converts the controller's output into physical action, here heat. The thermistor is the sensor, the microcontroller is the controller and the room is the plant.

questions.questionText: Which statement about open-loop control is NOT correct?
options: It automatically corrects the output when a disturbance acts on the plant
It is simpler and cheaper because no output sensor is needed
Its accuracy depends on how well it is calibrated
It cannot be destabilised by feedback, because it has none
questions.explanation: An open-loop controller never measures the output, so it cannot notice or correct a disturbance. The other three statements are true.

questions.questionText: A unity-feedback temperature loop uses a proportional controller with Kp = 4 driving a plant whose DC gain is 2. The setpoint is stepped up by 10 °C. What is the steady-state error?
questions.explanation: Loop gain K = Kp × plant gain = 8, so e_ss = 10/(1 + 8) = 1.11 °C and the output rises by 8.89 °C. 1.25 °C comes from 10/K, and zero error would need integral action.

questions.questionText: In a cruise-control system, what is the car itself (engine, drivetrain and body), whose speed is being controlled, called?
options: The plant (process)
The controller
The feedback element
The reference input
questions.explanation: The plant is the physical system whose output, vehicle speed, is controlled. The controller computes the throttle command, the feedback element is the speed sensor and the reference input is the set speed.

questions.questionText: In a negative-feedback loop with a very large loop gain (GH ≫ 1), which statement is correct?
options: The closed-loop gain is approximately G, so accuracy depends mainly on the plant
The closed-loop gain is approximately 1/H, so the overall accuracy depends mainly on the feedback sensor
The closed-loop gain approaches zero
The closed-loop gain is approximately GH
questions.explanation: T = G/(1 + GH) ≈ G/(GH) = 1/H when GH ≫ 1. Changes in G then matter little, but the loop can be no more accurate than its sensor.

questions.questionText: A room heater is controlled by a proportional-only (P) controller in a unity-feedback loop. Why does the room temperature settle slightly below the setpoint?
options: The heater needs a non-zero drive to replace the heat losses, and a P controller produces drive only from a non-zero error
The sensor always reads low when proportional control is used
The proportional gain is too low for the loop to be stable
The rate of change of the error is zero in steady state, which switches the heater off
questions.explanation: With u = Kp·e a steady heater output needs a steady error; the offset shrinks as Kp rises (e_ss = 1/(1 + K) of the step) but never reaches zero. Adding integral action removes it.

questions.questionText: In a negative-feedback loop with reference input r and feedback signal b, what is the actuating error signal produced by the summing junction?
options: e = r + b
e = b − r
e = r − b
e = r × b
questions.explanation: With negative feedback the fed-back signal is subtracted from the reference, so e = r − b. Adding the two signals would be positive feedback.

questions.questionText: A water heater uses on-off control with setpoint 60 °C and hysteresis of ±2 °C, so it switches ON at 58 °C and OFF at 62 °C. The heater is currently ON and the water has risen to 61 °C. What happens next?
options: The heater switches OFF immediately because 61 °C is above the setpoint
The heater stays ON until the water reaches 62 °C
The heater reduces its power in proportion to the 1 °C error
The heater switches rapidly OFF and ON around 60 °C
questions.explanation: With hysteresis the output changes only at the band edges, ON at 58 °C and OFF at 62 °C, and keeps its last state in between. This is what prevents relay chatter around the setpoint.

questions.questionText: A unity-feedback loop with a P controller drives a plant of DC gain 0.5. What is the minimum Kp that keeps the steady-state error to a step within 2% of the step size?
questions.explanation: 1/(1 + K) ≤ 0.02 requires loop gain K ≥ 49, and K = Kp × 0.5, so Kp ≥ 98. 49 is the loop gain itself, 100 drops the 1 in 1 + K, and 24.5 multiplies by the plant gain instead of dividing.

questions.questionText: What is the transfer function of a linear time-invariant system?
options: The ratio of output to input measured in the time domain at t = 1 s
The Laplace transform of the output when the input is a unit step
The difference between the setpoint and the output in the frequency domain
The ratio of the Laplace transform of the output to that of the input, with all initial conditions zero
questions.explanation: G(s) = C(s)/R(s) with zero initial conditions depends only on the system, not on the input applied. The step-response option describes C(s) for one particular input and the last option describes the error signal.

questions.questionText: A P controller with a bias (manual reset) of 40% and gain Kp = 5% per °C holds an oven at 66 °C while the setpoint is 70 °C. Using u = u0 + Kp·e, what is the controller output?
questions.explanation: e = 70 − 66 = 4 °C, so u = 40 + 5 × 4 = 60%. Subtracting the P term gives 20%, ignoring it gives 40% and adding the error without the gain gives 44%.

questions.questionText: A discrete PID controller runs with sampling period T = 0.01 s and Kd = 0.05 s. The error was 2.0 at the previous sample and is 1.8 now. What is the derivative term Kd(e[k] − e[k−1])/T?
questions.explanation: D = 0.05 × (1.8 − 2.0)/0.01 = 0.05 × (−20) = −1.0. Forgetting to divide by T gives −0.01, reversing the difference gives +1.0 and leaving out Kd gives −20.

questions.questionText: An on-off controller, whose output is either fully ON or fully OFF, is also known as a:
options: Proportional-derivative controller
Two-position (bang-bang) controller
Integral controller
Feedforward controller
questions.explanation: On-off control switches the actuator between two states only, hence the names two-position or bang-bang control. P, I and D controllers produce a continuously variable output.

questions.questionText: The error applied to a PID controller stays constant at a non-zero value. What does the derivative term contribute?
options: A constant output proportional to the error
An output that grows steadily with time
Nothing, because the error is not changing
An output equal to Kd times the error
questions.explanation: The derivative term responds only to de/dt, which is zero for a constant error. A constant contribution is the P term's behaviour and a steadily growing one is the I term's.

questions.questionText: An on-off water heater switches ON at 58 °C and OFF at 62 °C. While ON the water warms at 0.5 °C/min; while OFF it cools at 0.25 °C/min. Ignoring any lag, what is the switching period (one ON plus one OFF interval)?
options: 8 min
16 min
12 min
24 min
questions.explanation: The band is 4 °C, so ON time = 4/0.5 = 8 min and OFF time = 4/0.25 = 16 min, giving a period of 24 min (duty cycle 33%). Using 2 °C instead of the full 4 °C band gives 12 min.

questions.questionText: A temperature loop's step response settles at 50 °C and reaches a peak of 56 °C. What is the percentage overshoot?
questions.explanation: Overshoot = (peak − final)/final × 100 = (56 − 50)/50 × 100 = 12%. Dividing by the peak gives 10.7%, and 6% simply quotes the 6 °C excess.

questions.questionText: In a stable proportional control loop, what normally happens when Kp is increased?
options: Rise time increases and overshoot decreases
The steady-state error becomes exactly zero
Rise time and steady-state error decrease, but overshoot increases
Overshoot and steady-state error both decrease with no side effects
questions.explanation: A higher Kp drives the plant harder, so the loop rises faster and leaves a smaller offset 1/(1 + K), but it overshoots more and can eventually become unstable. Only integral action gives zero step error.

questions.questionText: What is integral windup in a PID loop, and what is the usual remedy?
options: The derivative term amplifies sensor noise; add a low-pass filter on the sensor
The integral becomes zero when the error is constant; increase Ki
The proportional term saturates the ADC; reduce the sampling rate
The integral keeps accumulating while the actuator is saturated, causing a large overshoot later; clamp the integral or stop integrating during saturation
questions.explanation: While the output is limited, extra integral action has no effect but keeps building, so the loop overshoots until the stored integral unwinds. Anti-windup limits or stops integration while the actuator is saturated.

questions.questionText: A motor speed response settles at 200 rpm. It passes 20 rpm at t = 0.3 s and 180 rpm at t = 1.1 s. What is the 10%–90% rise time?
questions.explanation: 10% and 90% of 200 rpm are 20 rpm and 180 rpm, so the rise time = 1.1 − 0.3 = 0.8 s. 1.1 s is measured from t = 0 and 1.4 s adds the two times.

questions.questionText: Why do many PID implementations apply the derivative action to the measured output rather than to the error, and low-pass filter it?
options: The derivative of the error is always zero in a closed loop
Differentiating the error gives a large spike when the setpoint steps, and differentiation amplifies high-frequency noise
Differentiating the output removes the steady-state error
It allows the derivative term to replace the integral term
questions.explanation: A setpoint step makes e jump, so de/dt is huge for one sample (derivative kick); the measured output changes smoothly, so differentiating it avoids the spike. Noise has a large slope, so the D term is also filtered.

questions.questionText: A discrete PI controller uses u[k] = Kp·e[k] + Ki·T·Σe[j] (sum from j = 0 to k) with Kp = 1.2, Ki = 0.5 s⁻¹ and T = 0.2 s. The errors at k = 0, 1 and 2 are 5, 3 and 2. What is u[2]?
questions.explanation: P = 1.2 × 2 = 2.4 and I = 0.5 × 0.2 × (5 + 3 + 2) = 1.0, so u[2] = 3.4. Forgetting T gives 7.4, leaving the current error out of the sum gives 3.2 and dropping the I term gives 2.4.

questions.questionText: A PID routine takes 120 µs to execute and is run every 1 ms by a timer interrupt. What fraction of CPU time does the control loop use?
questions.explanation: Utilisation = execution time/period = 120 µs/1000 µs = 0.12 = 12%. 88% is the time left for other work, and 8.3 comes from inverting the ratio (1000/120).

questions.questionText: What is the main risk of choosing a sampling period that is too long for a digital control loop?
options: The integral term can no longer remove steady-state error
The extra delay adds phase lag, reducing the stability margin and causing oscillation or instability
The ADC resolution in bits decreases
The time constant of the plant becomes longer
questions.explanation: A slow loop acts on old information, which behaves like added loop delay and lowers the gain at which oscillation starts. Sampling well faster than the plant time constants avoids this.

questions.questionText: In what order should a periodic digital control task perform its work in each sampling period?
options: Read the sensor (ADC) → compute the error and control law → write the actuator output (PWM/DAC) → wait for the next tick
Write the actuator output → compute the control law → read the sensor → wait for the next tick
Compute the control law → read the sensor → wait for the next tick → write the actuator output
Read the sensor → write the actuator output → wait for the next tick → compute the control law
questions.explanation: The control law needs a fresh measurement, and the result should be output as soon as it is computed to keep the delay between sampling and actuation small.

questions.questionText: A control task is started by a timer interrupt. The timer is clocked at 1 MHz and interrupts every 5000 counts. What are the sampling period and sampling frequency?
options: 5 ms and 200 Hz
0.5 ms and 2 kHz
50 ms and 20 Hz
5 µs and 200 kHz
questions.explanation: Each count takes 1/1 MHz = 1 µs, so T = 5000 × 1 µs = 5 ms and f = 1/T = 200 Hz.

questions.questionText: Why is a digital PID routine normally triggered by a periodic timer interrupt (or a high-priority periodic RTOS task) rather than run in a free-running main loop?
options: Timer interrupts make each ADC conversion more accurate
A free-running loop cannot use floating-point arithmetic
Interrupt-driven control removes the need for anti-windup
The discrete integral and derivative terms assume a constant sampling period T, so the timing must be fixed and jitter-free
questions.explanation: Ki·T·Σe and Kd(e[k] − e[k−1])/T are only correct if samples are exactly T apart, while a free-running loop's period varies with the other work it does. Jitter in T acts like noise and extra delay in the loop.

questions.questionText: A velocity-form PID uses Δu[k] = Kp(e[k] − e[k−1]) + Ki·T·e[k] + (Kd/T)(e[k] − 2e[k−1] + e[k−2]) and u[k] = u[k−1] + Δu[k], with Kp = 2, Ki = 1 s⁻¹, Kd = 0.1 s and T = 0.1 s. The errors are e[0] = 4, e[1] = 3 and e[2] = 2.5, and u[1] = 5.7. What is u[2]?
questions.explanation: Δu = 2(2.5 − 3) + 1(0.1)(2.5) + (0.1/0.1)(2.5 − 6 + 4) = −1 + 0.25 + 0.5 = −0.25, so u[2] = 5.7 − 0.25 = 5.45. Dropping the integral term gives 5.2, using a first difference in the D term gives 4.45 and forgetting T in the integral term gives 7.7.

questions.questionText: In a feedback control system with forward-path gain G and feedback-path gain H, what is meant by the loop gain?
options: The ratio G/H of forward gain to feedback gain
The closed-loop gain G/(1 + GH)
The product GH, the gain a signal sees travelling once around the loop
The sum G + H of the two path gains
questions.explanation: The loop gain GH is the gain around the loop from the summing junction back to itself. It sets how strongly feedback acts: the closed-loop gain is G/(1 + GH), and sensitivity and output disturbances are reduced by the factor 1 + GH.

questions.questionText: A plant G(s) = 10/(s + 2) is placed in a unity negative-feedback loop. What is the closed-loop transfer function?
questions.explanation: T = G/(1 + G) = [10/(s + 2)] / [(s + 12)/(s + 2)] = 10/(s + 12), with DC gain 10/12 = 0.83. 10/(s − 8) is the positive-feedback result.

questions.questionText: Adding derivative action to a proportional controller mainly:
options: Improves damping and reduces overshoot
Eliminates the steady-state error to a step input
Increases the steady-state gain of the loop
Removes the need for a feedback sensor
questions.explanation: The derivative term opposes rapid changes of the error, adding damping and reducing overshoot. It gives nothing for a constant error, so it cannot remove steady-state error; that is the integral term's job.

questions.questionText: A continuous-time closed-loop LTI system is stable if and only if:
options: All open-loop zeros lie in the right half of the s-plane
All closed-loop poles (roots of 1 + G(s)H(s) = 0) have negative real parts
The open-loop DC gain is greater than 1
At least one closed-loop pole lies on the positive real axis
questions.explanation: Poles in the left half-plane give exponentially decaying terms, so a bounded input produces a bounded output. A pole with a positive real part gives a growing term and instability.

questions.questionText: A loop oscillates steadily at the ultimate gain Ku = 10 with period Pu = 2 s. Using the Ziegler–Nichols closed-loop PID rules Kp = 0.6Ku, Ti = Pu/2 and Td = Pu/8, what are the parallel-form gains Kp, Ki = Kp/Ti and Kd = Kp·Td?
options: Kp = 6, Ki = 1 s⁻¹, Kd = 0.25 s
Kp = 5, Ki = 5 s⁻¹, Kd = 1.25 s
Kp = 6, Ki = 6 s⁻¹, Kd = 1.5 s
questions.explanation: Kp = 0.6 × 10 = 6, Ti = 2/2 = 1 s and Td = 2/8 = 0.25 s, so Ki = 6/1 = 6 s⁻¹ and Kd = 6 × 0.25 = 1.5 s. Quoting Ti and Td as the gains, or dividing them by Kp, are the usual slips.

questions.questionText: A unity-feedback loop has G(s) = K/(s(s + 4)). For K = 3, where are the closed-loop poles?
options: s = 0 and s = −4
s = −1 and s = −3 (stable)
s = +1 and s = +3 (unstable)
questions.explanation: 1 + G(s) = 0 gives s² + 4s + 3 = (s + 1)(s + 3) = 0, so the poles are −1 and −3, both in the left half-plane. 0 and −4 are the open-loop poles, and −2 ± j1.73 would need K = 7.

questions.questionText: A first-order plant G(s) = 2/(10s + 1) is controlled by a P controller with Kp = 2 in a unity-feedback loop. What are the closed-loop time constant and the approximate 2% settling time (take 4 time constants)?
options: 10 s and 40 s
2.5 s and 10 s
2 s and 8 s
questions.explanation: The loop gain is K = 2 × 2 = 4, so T(s) = 4/(10s + 5) = 0.8/(2s + 1): τ_cl = 10/(1 + 4) = 2 s and t_s ≈ 4 × 2 = 8 s. 10 s is the open-loop time constant, 2.5 s uses τ/K and 3.33 s ignores the plant gain.

questions.questionText: A sampled plant obeys y[k+1] = 0.9·y[k] + 0.1·u[k] and is controlled by u[k] = Kp(r − y[k]). For which range of positive Kp is the closed loop stable?
options: Any positive Kp
questions.explanation: Substituting gives y[k+1] = (0.9 − 0.1Kp)·y[k] + 0.1Kp·r, a single pole at 0.9 − 0.1Kp. Stability needs |0.9 − 0.1Kp| < 1, i.e. −1 < Kp < 19; Kp < 9 only keeps the pole positive so the response does not alternate in sign.

u = 100, integ = 30
u = 150, integ = 90
u = 120, integ = 60
questions.explanation: Pass 1: integ = 30 and u = 60 + 30 = 90. In passes 2 and 3 integ would reach 60 and u = 120, so u is clamped to 100 and integ is restored to 30; without anti-windup integ would have wound up to 90.
